item.title: ALLFED’s 2026 Highlights
item.description:
Published on November 13, 2026 11:04 AM GMT

Welcome to Alliance to Feed the Earth (ALLFED)’s 2026 Highlights, our annual reflection on how we advanced the organization’s mission, helping governments and other decision-makers strengthen the resilience of global food systems to catastrophic risks through research, policy, and practical action. 

This year, ALLFED made significant progress on several fronts: strengthening our leadership and global team, publishing research and conducting pilots that continue to deepen the evidence base and expand the field of food-system resilience, and working with governments and partners to improve preparedness for global catastrophic food-system shocks. The sections below also highlight our public engagement, fundraising, and team.

We also refreshed our website to make our work easier to explore, with clearer ways to engage.

As the year-end giving season approaches, we’ll share a call for support during Marginal Funding Week on the EA Forum, starting November 16. From December, gifts to ALLFED will be matched dollar for dollar until the $20,000 pool is reached. In the meantime, you can continue to support our work here.

ALLFED’s next chapter

New CEO: Yushuwa Nettles

In May 2026, Yushuwa Nettles joined ALLFED as CEO, bringing nearly 20 years of experience across diplomacy, international development, government and the private sector. His work has included serving as a U.S. diplomat, addressing political and human-rights issues in Kenya, and holding senior executive roles at USAID-supported programs in Tunisia, Libya and Iraq.

His experience is directly relevant to ALLFED’s mission, where food security is closely connected to governance, national security and social stability. Under Yushuwa’s leadership, we will continue advancing research on how catastrophic events could disrupt food systems, and the practical solutions that could keep food available for everyone, while strengthening the partnerships, systems and operational capacity needed to bring that work closer to governments, institutions and communities. 

In line with this effort, Yushuwa and the team have developed ALLFED’s new tabletop exercises, which aim to put decision-makers inside global catastrophe scenarios to test how agencies could work together to keep food available to people around the world. 

Reach out for a conversation, or to request a facilitated tabletop exercise tailored to your context. 

Research: understanding risks and developing solutions

Research remains at the heart of ALLFED’s work. Despite working with a leaner team, our team produced eight new research submissions, bringing our total output to more than 80 publications and reports since ALLFED began. Some of the year's most notable work includes:

Leaf protein biorefineries could help provide food after a catastrophe

Our peer-reviewed paper, “Global potential of integrated biorefineries for leaf protein and sugar: Producing sustainable food and preventing starvation in catastrophes” was published in Sustainable Production and Consumption.

The research models leaf protein concentrate biorefineries as viable global food infrastructure: affordable to build, fast to scale and capable of sustaining protein supply even under extreme agricultural disruption. 

Our research estimates that, with rapid deployment, factories producing leaf protein concentrate could meet global protein requirements within only one to two years. Production of both leaf protein and sugar could supply around 5% of global calorie needs in just one year. Because grasslands can support these crops (e.g. clover or alfalfa) even where conventional food crops are difficult to grow, they could provide an important source of food when conventional agriculture is severely disrupted. The modeling suggests that grassland-derived leaf protein could meet global protein needs even in extreme nuclear-winter scenarios, and food produced through these systems could cost a mere $1–2 per person per day to provide all daily energy needs. 

The paper generated media coverage across outlets, including Vegconomist, TIME, and Protein Production Technology, with the latter a profile of ALLFED Research Manager Juan García Martínez. Juan and Ross Milne, CEO of leaf protein company Leaft Foods, also co-wrote an op-ed on The Plant Base, examining what ALLFED’s LPC research findings mean for the protein industry today.

Research pending peer-review

Testing crops under simulated nuclear-winter conditions

Researcher Simon Blouin and his team, in collaboration with Penn State University, studied the viability of staple crops under the low-light and low-temperature conditions simulated for a post-nuclear war "nuclear winter." They used growth chambers to replicate both tropical and temperate environments to see if these crops could still produce food. Simon explains:    

“This was the first study of its kind. Every assessment of how much food the world could grow during a nuclear winter has so far rested on crop models that were never tested under the conditions they're supposed to predict. Nobody had ever grown a staple crop, from seed to harvest, under simulated nuclear-winter light and temperature.

We grew wheat, canola, and potato for a full season in chambers reproducing what climate models predict for a tropical location (Indonesia) and a temperate location (South Australia) during the worst year of a worst-case nuclear winter.” 

Pilot results showed viable tropical yields, while temperate stem collapse revealed a failure mode crop models miss, strengthening the case for scaling up experiments.

“The stem collapse we observed in the low-light temperate chamber was an unexpected and important finding. This is exactly the kind of finding we want in hand before a catastrophe, while there's still time to test more crops and identify which hold up. There are dozens of crops that should be screened in the same way; the results could shape how billions of people survive an abrupt sunlight reduction scenario.” 

Read about the experiment, and support scaling up this critical research.

 

Food security and AMOC collapse

The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a key ocean current that spans the Atlantic and plays an important role in regulating our current climate, with an impact well beyond the Atlantic itself. A substantial weakening or collapse could disrupt temperatures and rainfall patterns across the world, with serious consequences for agriculture. In our preprint paper, we carry out initial crop modeling on the impacts of an AMOC collapse. 

The study finds that total wheat, maize, and rice yields worldwide would fall by 5.3%. However, there is a strong regional element to this, and yield losses would range from 12% to 19% across key countries like Canada, India and China. This would raise food prices by 17-40%, make the world more reliant on trade, and threaten nutritional access for some of the most vulnerable. This was the first study using a rigorous crop model for AMOC collapse, offering a more grounded assessment of its potentially serious agricultural impacts. 

This research has received significant media attention, including coverage in Live Science, Popular Mechanics (syndicated in Yahoo News) as well as other high-traffic media outlets. 

Our work is only the beginning.  Support us as we investigate how climate change and food-system shifts could shape our exposure to AMOC collapse and the additional volatility and damage it could cause.

More research highlights from 2026

  • “No Place to Hide? Regional Resilience and Vulnerability to Global Catastrophic Risk”: This peer-reviewed paper published in Global Challenges examines which countries are best able to withstand a global catastrophe. It concludes that no country is resilient to every threat, but Australia performs strongly across many scenarios. The research received considerable mainstream media coverage, including from ABC Australia, The New Daily, and the UK newspaper The Times. The work helps the public understand a wider range of catastrophes and shows that strengthening regional resilience requires investment in food-systems, critical infrastructure, and coordinated trade.
  • “Calculating equilibrium cereal prices during a multi-year productivity shock”: Models how global cereal markets would respond to a protracted agricultural productivity shock to better understand how economic incentives and policy responses could reduce the impact. The modeling finds that cereal prices could rise more than tenfold in some scenarios, with accurate forecasting of the shock's severity emerging as a critical factor in minimizing harm to low-income populations worldwide.
  • “Scaling up irrigation for food-system resilience under abrupt sunlight reduction”: Analyzes how expanded groundwater irrigation, combined with cropland expansion, could help offset agricultural losses under an abrupt sunlight-reduction scenario.
  • “Assessment of temporary housing for on-site isolation of essential workers during extreme pandemics”: Assesses whether hotels, trailers, converted vans, etc. could provide temporary accommodation for workers needed to maintain critical services given that, in a severe pandemic, the people keeping power, water and food running may need to live at work. The study finds that pooling resources worldwide could house most workers, but nearly half of countries could not do so independently.
  • “Psychological Demand of Catastrophic Risk: A Framework for Mental and Behavioural Resilience Under Systemic Disruption”: Builds a novel framework mapping how stressors degrade psychological functioning across four collapse substages, arguing that psychological capacity is a structural prerequisite for societal stability.
  • “The largest crop production shocks: magnitude, causes and frequency” was selected as a Highlight Paper by Earth System Dynamics, the editors acknowledging that the work shows massive crop failures—averaging nearly 30% and sometimes reaching 80%—that have already happened repeatedly in the real world. The work also featured as an EGU (European Geosciences Union) Journals highlight in February.

Policy and preparedness

Alongside our research, we continued working with governments, organizations and other partners to turn food-system resilience into practical preparedness. 2026 Policy highlights include:

Contributing to UN thinking on nuclear war and food resilience

In December 2025, ALLFED collaborator Florian Ulrich Jehn presented ALLFED’s work to the United Nations Independent Scientific Panel on the Effects of Nuclear War, outlining potential impacts on global food systems and ways to strengthen resilience. At the Panel’s request, he submitted a formal written contribution in January 2026.

ALLFED Head of Policy Noah Wescombe also presented to the UN Independent Scientific Panel on the Effects of Nuclear War, delivering his presentation in person in Bangkok in October.

U.S.: Emergency flexibility in biofuel policy

Through ALLFED’s U.S. Biofuels Engagement Program, we are building a coalition of partners from trade associations and corporate government affairs teams, through to federal agencies to build support for emergency flexibility in renewable fuel policy. 

The legal and administrative pathways exist—the US Environmental Protection Agency has broad authority under the Clean Air Act to waive or reduce renewable fuel obligations. The challenge is building the political support to use them when food security is at stake. ALLFED’s strategy is to build a coalition of partners with genuine food security exposure who would advocate for emergency flexibility if conditions warranted it.

Brazil: Protecting progress on hunger

We developed a policy brief for Brazilian policymakers, “Protecting Brazil's Hunger Gains Against Climate and Food-System Shocks.”

Brazil left the FAO Hunger Map in 2025, an important achievement. But progress on hunger could be threatened by climate-related shocks, including floods, droughts and extreme heat.

Our central message is that protecting progress on hunger requires making food systems more resilient before a crisis occurs, and the brief recommends strengthening social protection, family farming, public procurement, urban climate adaptation and decentralized food reserves. It also considers how Brazil's agricultural and bioeconomy sectors, including sugarcane fermentation, could contribute to resilience in severe scenarios.

ALLFED Australia: Growing Rural Resilience

Our sister organization ALLFED Australia is bringing ALLFED’s mission to life through the Growing Rural Resilience project, a two-year pilot in the Wimmera region. The project is supported by the Australian Government’s National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA) through the Disaster Ready Fund and philanthropic sources such as Coefficient Giving, and delivered by ALLFED Australia in partnership with ALLFED Institute, Plant Health Australia, 3EC Consulting, and the Long Game Project. 

The project uses scenario-based planning to help agricultural producers and regional institutions prepare for cascading and compounding disasters, bringing together stakeholders whose responsibilities often span different government departments, industries and local organizations.

The project has already involved a workshop with 13 farmers, tours of local farms and interviews with growers to document operational constraints in dryland cropping systems during severe stress events, such as the conflict in Iran and resulting fuel, production and trade disruptions. Next, cross-sector representatives will explore how the region could respond to major disruptions, as well as test a key question: Can resilience strategies be understood, adopted and acted on across the entire agricultural value chain? 

Public engagement highlights

More coverage of ALLFED’s work

  • Forbes Sustainability featured ALLFED’s 2025 paper on pandemic risk in “Preparing For The Next Pandemic,” noting that “it was awarded ‘Best Paper’ last year for laying out where preparing for a pandemic is most important.”
  • Florian Jehn’s article, “How nuclear war would impact the global food system. And how to prepare for it” was featured in the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists’ “Nuclear winter: Why study it now?” series. It highlights practical measures to strengthen food system resilience and prevent catastrophic food shortages in the event of nuclear war.
  • NHK Documentary: ALLFED is set to feature in a documentary series produced by NHK World, the national broadcaster in Japan. It will explore the scenario of a comet collision with Japan, and the work of organizations like ALLFED to build resilience to these types of catastrophic events. Scheduled for release in early 2027 in Japan (with a future U.S. release date later in 2027), this is an important opportunity to help educate the public about global catastrophic risks.
  • Food from the air: ALLFED was featured in Forbes Russia, in an article exploring how scientists can produce fats, proteins and carbohydrates without relying on conventional plants or animals—and the potential of novel food technologies for strengthening food-system resilience.
  • Preparing for extreme weather: ALLFED Senior Economist Michael Hinge spoke to Live Science about the potential food-security implications of a strong El Niño, including how extreme weather could affect food supplies and why households may need to consider preparedness.
  • Feeding the world in catastrophe: David was featured on RNZ’s Our Changing World podcast as well as their Raising the Bar lecture series, both opportunities to amplify ALLFED’s work to a broader audience.

Events Highlights 

  • Research Manager Juan García Martínez presented at Food Biomanufacturing for National Security in June, a joint symposium by GFI-ETI, followed by a congressional reception at the U.S. Capitol. The event focused on how food-grade biomanufacturing infrastructure can serve national security needs, connecting to ALLFED’s work demonstrating how existing infrastructure can be leveraged to feed people in a catastrophe.
  • ALLFED Co-founder and Research Director David Denkenberger spoke at NASA Ames Research Centre in California’s Silicon Valley about resilient food systems for space missions and presented at the EA chapter of the University of California, Berkeley. He also supported Head of Policy Noah Wescombe’s Extreme Pandemic Resilience workshop at EAGx San Francisco.
  • Juan and Florian presented at the World Adaptation Forum 2026 in April, an event focused on systemic risk, societal collapse and adaptation, and both interviews are featured on the event’s YouTube channel.
  • David, Luisa Lopes Monteiro, Pinkeshkumar Attarwala, and Mohammadreza Ebrahimnataj Tiji took part in an informal presentation to Islands for the Future of Humanity in Christchurch, New Zealand, discussing ALLFED’s work on food-system resilience.
  • At EAG London in May, Sonia Cassidy, Mike Hinge, and Amanda Cassidy welcomed visitors to our stall and shared more about ALLFED’s work. Dorine Ukah, a key member of our team in Africa, represented ALLFED at the EA Summit Nigeria in July.
  • David presented at the EA Summit Wellington, New Zealand in September, leading two workshops. He also gave three talks at Western University, Ontario, Canada, increasing exposure to ALLFED research as well as organization recognition and opportunities for collaboration.
  • Research Manager Juan García Martínez also presented ALLFED’s CO₂-to-food research at the Gordon Research Conference: Future Foods, on emerging ways to make food much more efficiently than photosynthesis.
  • UPCOMING: David and Pinkesh will present at EAGx Australasia in Melbourne, 27 to 29 November. If you’re planning to be there, we encourage you to connect with them!

Fundraising

In 2026, ALLFED continued building a more structured approach to fundraising, increased direct engagement with supporters, and developed a Fundraising Priorities Portfolio to give prospective donors a clearer picture of ALLFED’s room for more funding, including priority research and implementation projects that additional support could advance.

Building on our 2025 year-end matching campaign, which raised nearly $50,000, we are preparing a broader year-end fundraising effort, kicking off with the Effective Altruism Forum’s Marginal Funding Week commencing Monday 16 November. This will be followed by our 2026 Match Opportunity, where all gifts will be matched dollar for dollar until the $20,000 matching pool is reached. Plus, of course, stay tuned for our Giving Tuesday and year-end giving campaigns. 

There are many ways that you can continue to support our work here, and your generosity is sincerely appreciated. These efforts are helping build the relationships and fundraising capacity needed to support ALLFED’s longer-term research and preparedness work.

Our Team

As of October 2026, our team currently spans nearly 30 countries around the world, and once again across all continents except Antarctica.

We are pleased to have welcomed Dr. Avianto Amri (senior research fellow of the Resilience Development Initiative and chairperson of the Indonesian Society for Disaster Management) and Dr. Catherine Rhodes (previously executive director of the Cambridge Centre for the Study of Existential Risk) as new Board of Advisors members. 

The past few years have tested ALLFED: like many organizations, we scaled back amid a volatile funding landscape, while retaining room for more funding. We have kept most of our experienced core team and preserved institutional knowledge. More than half of our founding team remain, around 40% of paid team members have been here for 5+ years, and our operational core has held together for nearly a decade. 

We also completed the first year of ALLFED’s two-year Gender Equality Plan (GEP) in April, an important step in improving diversity and strengthening the organization in order to better serve its mission.  

Thank you

This year’s progress has been a collective effort, and we’re grateful to our team members, volunteers, partners, supporters, and donors who make it possible, and for the time, expertise, and commitment they’ve brought to this work. Thank you to everyone who contributed to ALLFED’s progress this year. 

Your support helps us work with governments and other decision-makers to strengthen the resilience of global food systems to catastrophic risks. Through research, policy, and practical action, we help build preparedness before a catastrophe and safeguard food access if one occurs.

Support ALLFED here

item.title: Don't Burn the Boats for Slower Worlds
item.description:
Published on November 13, 2026 12:11 PM GMT

[Epistemic Status: Fairly confident that this is a problem, low confidence on what to do about it]

TL;DR:

Updates towards short timelines based on METR's November 2026 report on AI R&D acceleration at Anthropic are rational, but based on limited public evidence. If things take longer than currently expected, the appearance of consensus in the AI safety community will likely be used by skeptics to (attempt to) discredit AI safety and justify unsafe policy. If timelines are off by only a few years, this discrediting will come right before the intelligence explosion actually happens. Because a large chunk of survival mass remains in worlds where things move slowly, it is important to come up with ways to mitigate this dynamic. 

Short timelines are in. The AI Futures Project declared that it "Looks Like the Intelligence Explosion Will Happen in 2027 After All," Jake Mendel of Coefficient Giving (who explicitly described himself as having had "substantially longer timelines than my friends at Anthropic" and conditioned his update on "if METR is correct here") said he expects a >50% chance of ASI in the next 18 months without a slowdown, and Buck Shlegeris of Redwood said that he now believes there is "about a one in three chance" of ASI within a year, primarily because of "research released this week by METR." These updates seem reasonable to me. My timelines were already fairly short, and got shorter as a result of METR's report, which found a 1.9x speedup to progress on Anthropic's internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index, and attributed it largely to AI involvement in the R&D process.

While the METR report points towards shortened timelines, the publicly available info does not necessitate them. Toby Ord, for instance, put out a case that the speedup shrinks to 1.4x once you account for a one-time bump from Mythos Preview's larger pretrain. (METR found a slope change accounted for the data better than a one-time jump, but did not publicly reject Ord's hypothesis, which includes both.) Including other labs' models also separately gives a 1.4x speedup, instead of the 1.9x for Anthropic models only. And the evidence against explanations other than AI speeding up research is mostly redacted. Much of the updating has been on AI responsibility for the speedup, and the evidence for that rests primarily on the judgement of the METR employees who saw the unredacted evidence rather than on public data.[1] Which is reasonable! METR is filled with brilliant and knowledgeable people with good epistemic hygiene, many of whom went in with (comparatively) slow timelines. But for lack of stronger evidence, the update of one group (and note that METR said that they "would not be surprised if the true acceleration was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate") has been metabolized by a much broader group. See this thread for a more in-depth discussion of this dynamic. 

I worry that, if it turns out that we have a bit more time than expected, this belief cascade will make the AI safety position weaker (there are also risks related to field building and resource allocation, but I'll focus on reputational hazards). For example, Tamay Besiroglu (Epoch and Mechanize co-founder, now at Google DeepMind):

It's a positive development that there's now some convergence in the AI risk community that there's likely an intelligence explosion next year. I think it'll be clear in a few years that this didn't happen, these people will be largely discredited, and discussions will become more sane.

Zvi Mowshowitz discusses this dynamic in AI #194:

A warning in advance: There are those who will say that if the world does not end or get radically transformed in 2027, that means that those who thought this was a possibility are now ‘discredited.’ Some will even then use that to try to dismiss all concerns about AI safety or any predictions of recursive self-improvement, forever. Some are even laying the groundwork for this now, in part to scare off people from making such warnings or taking them seriously. This is despite those same people usually having been continuously wrong about AI capabilities, and those worried about AI now having previously been shockingly accurate.

Do not fall for this. It is logically wrong and usually in deeply bad faith. Some credibility should of course be lost, but on the order of Nate Silver’s lost credibility if Hillary Clinton had won in 2016, when he was giving Donald Trump a real chance whereas others thought Clinton was 99%. If you give a well-calibrated and continuously updated probability distribution, half the time events will happen later than your median, and most of the time events will happen later than the earliest median you ever predict.

While Zvi is right that this would be blatantly unfair (as both Toby Ord and David Krueger point out, most numbers are probabilities, not certainties), that hasn't stopped similar incidents in the past.[2] Labs, looking to ward off a potentially regulation-friendly incoming administration in 2029, may point to the doomers' failed predictions of foom as a way to discredit the AI safety movement as a whole. Regulators or legislators, especially those who have been sympathetic to AI safety in part on the basis of arguments from AI safety people's forecasting track records, may see evidence that the whole thing is bunk. These sorts of societal dynamics are hard to predict but there is clearly a risk here, and there will almost certainly be people who at least attempt to exploit any failed prediction. This would be especially damaging if timelines are only off by a few years; confidence in AI safety forecasters would be at its lowest right as we actually began a takeoff.

Of course, not having an intelligence explosion in 2028 would do little to falsify the broader AI risk case. It would give us more time to coordinate, do alignment and control and interp research, and at absolute worst give us more time before the axe falls, but the basic question of whether superintelligent AI (or narrowly superhuman AI in domains like cyber and bio) poses massive risks to humanity is unaffected by when takeoff happens. More time improves our odds but doesn't change the basic case.

Furthermore, because of the improved odds from slower timelines, a good chunk of survival mass comes in worlds where timelines are slower than they currently appear. Just as an example (I don't endorse these specific numbers):

YMMV on how strong a consideration this is, and it's very sensitive to individual beliefs on timelines, alignment tractability, short- and medium-term coordination difficulty, and geopolitics, but it seems at least somewhat relevant for almost everyone. Furthermore, there may be even more leverage in slower worlds, because there would be more time for protracted policy fights, where track record would be very likely to play a role. 

Right now, it seems like a lot of communication is geared towards worlds with short timelines. I think this is reasonable for two main reasons:

  1. If you genuinely believe timelines are short, there are deontic reasons to communicate that as forcefully and clearly as you can. There's something slimy about playing 4D chess with communicating about an imminent intelligence explosion. And, even if it is morally acceptable, this kind of galaxy-brained thinking is rarely wise.
  2. If a near-term slowdown is tractable, that should clearly be a top priority. It helps in long timeline worlds and it is arguably necessary in short timeline ones. Emphasizing the urgency of the situation and how little time may be left seems as good a way as any to make that happen.

So what's the solution? How do you clearly and honestly communicate your well-founded beliefs about near-term progress without burning the boats for slower worlds? I don't know. To some extent this is an unavoidable tradeoff, and for the reasons above I don't think that the solution is to overly hedge communications. A few steps, in rough order of my confidence that they'd help:

  1. Anthropic should release much more information. This seems good for unrelated reasons (see e.g. METR, who say that "this report does not achieve ‘transparency about evidence’"). But it also opens up two possibilities:
    1. The redacted evidence will bear out METR's subjective conclusions and reduce outsiders' credences in longer timelines, allowing a clear focus on preventing and/or dealing with an imminent intelligence explosion without worrying as much about slower worlds.
    2. The evidence will be more ambiguous and there will be less clustering, so that if timelines are in fact longer, a large subset of reliable AI safety people will still have their credibility fully intact.

This doesn't seem incredibly tractable for the typical person, but would definitely be nice! If the information is too sensitive to release publicly, as Anthropic claims, it could still be shared with more independent organizations so that METR doesn't have to shoulder all the epistemic weight.

  1. Talk about things that are unambiguously happening. The rate of progress (on benchmarks that seem at least somewhat correlated to general capabilities) is increasing. Maybe that's not due to AI and/or won't start imminently compounding. But it's still a massive deal! Progress was already extremely fast and it's hard to tell at what point we'll reach scary capabilities (and we already have in cyber). Even in slow worlds, short-term action is good. AI seems to be speeding up the AI R&D process in some way (what Dean Ball calls "weak recursion"), at minimum by streamlining coding tasks. And there are credible reasons to believe in an imminent intelligence explosion, and yet lab transparency is weak.[3] These are all problems regardless of timelines.
  2. Emphasize uncertainty where applicable. Those who want to argue in bad faith still will, but it is cheap to make it more difficult for them (and of course to make it easier for people who are trying their best to reason in good faith). Ord's call for explicit probabilities is a good starting point here.
  3. Keep thinking about what to do in worlds where things are slower. How do we frame things in those worlds? What are the actions that will be rational to take in 2028 if we haven't had an intelligence explosion yet, and what should we do now to set ourselves up for those actions? Again, I have limited thoughts here, and welcome any comments and ideas.

The METR report is scary. The world is scary. We may well be on the brink of scary progress on the scale of months. Or we may not be. Individually rational updates may collectively weaken our position in the ~1/3 to 2/3 of worlds where we have longer. Regardless of whether or not one has Broad Timelines, it is wise to act in a way that works broadly. 

Thanks to Claude Opus 5.5 for research assistance and feedback on drafts; all writing and views are my own.

  1. ^

    For example: Ryan Greenblatt, "I do trust the authors of the report a lot to be careful and rigorous"; Ajeya Cotra,  "I trust that my colleagues did a careful and rigorous job" (both Greenblatt and Cotra work at METR, but did not have access to the unredacted report); Eli Lifland, "I feel compelled to update nearly all the way to their result given that I respect the people who did the assessment," and the AIFP authors collectively, "we're mostly trusting the METR team here" (AIFP). 

  2. ^

    One example is AIFP, who were heavily criticized when they moved their timelines back, even though, conditional on METR being right, AI R&D is now moving faster than the original AI 2027 timelines!

  3. ^

    To be fair to Anthropic, they are doing more transparency-wise than the other labs, and have (via cofounder Sam McCandlish) announced that "In the coming weeks, we plan to share a report with our own analysis of the speed of AI progress within Anthropic." I think it's important not to punish labs for doing more of the right thing than others. As in many such cases, Anthropic is ahead of the competition, but behind where it ideally would be.

item.title: How we turned the EA Introductory Fellowship into an accredited course at our university
item.description:
Published on November 13, 2026 12:12 PM GMT

TL;DR:

  • We contacted our university about introducing the EA Introductory Fellowship as a one-credit elective in a program of our Economics bachelor’s degree.
  • They were happy to do it, and we ran it with 27 students. We were paid €1800 for it, and will continue offering it for the foreseeable future.
  • Past Economics students received the credit retroactively, and now all our fellowships offer one credit to eligible students.
  • We think this might be low-hanging fruit for other university groups as well, and would like to strongly encourage them to look for similar opportunities.

This spring, we at PISE (Positive Impact Society Erasmus) introduced the EA Introductory Fellowship as a one-credit elective at Erasmus University Rotterdam, a well-ranked Dutch university with a strong economics department. The ultimate goal in our theory of change is to get as many students as possible to do the most good they can, primarily through impactful careers and earning-to-give. The fellowship is how most of the students at our school become familiar with effective altruism and eventually become active in the community (and if you’re organizing a student group and not running a fellowship, you should seriously consider it. It’s a great way to communicate ideas in a high-fidelity manner that sticks).

The same is true for most other student groups, so if you’re already running a fellowship, it’s worth checking if you can get your fellowship accredited since most of the work is already done. An accredited course is a great way to significantly extend reach and improve the reputation of student groups. For us, the effort to get our fellowship accredited was surprisingly low (~4 meetings with the university, including the necessary preparation). We want to share how and why we did it in order to inspire and encourage other groups to find ways to do the same.

Why you should get your fellowship accredited if you can

The main advantages we found were:

  1. The course gains a renewed sense of authority. We could now frame the fellowship more similarly to existing academic courses.
    • You can expect people to take the course more seriously (reflected in better preparation, engagement, and attendance). This reduces the need to bring people up to speed on the concepts (although a recap is still beneficial), and improves the quality of discussions and the overall experience.
    • You’re guaranteed people’s attention from the first to the last session, thanks to lower dropout rates. You have more time to build arguments, and can now build the course up in a more structured way. For example, you no longer have to front-load the fun stuff (games, interesting topics, speakers) just to get people to stick around.
    • You might be able to create a course page (such as a Canvas page) and a syllabus. You should make these appealing, as they are how students form their first impressions and expectations. You will be able to set deadlines and expectations around submissions, which you can communicate by invoking consequences (e.g., you are required to submit discussion notes every week in order to pass the course), and possibly introduce grading (more on this later).
  2. It improves the standing of your group. Having an accredited course is a great conversation starter and reputation booster, which can be used to help organize talks, workshops, or collaborations with the university or other organizations.
  3. You can get an academic supervisor to help review and improve the course. We were able to discuss our curriculum with a professor who was our academic supervisor, which exposed the professor to EA ideas and improved our curriculum at the same time.
  4. It’s an upskilling opportunity for board members/organizers and facilitators. An accredited course is a chance to upskill in areas such as organization (setting up a university course), pitching (preparing and perfecting proposals to university staff), or content knowledge and communication (building the course and giving feedback). Being a university course coordinator is also a great CV booster and lets you build personal connections within the university.
  5. You can obtain funding for your group. Your group might get paid by your university. We received €60 per student (€60 * 30 = €1800), which we used to help finance our group. I would guess that it postponed our CEA Group Support Grants application by 6–12 months.
  6. It can extend to your regular fellowship. Once the course was accredited, all eligible Economics students who had completed our fellowship before received the credit retroactively, and all our fellowships now count for one credit for Economics students.

How to get started and make a good first impression

Here we talk about what we learned about the process of getting the fellowship accredited and how we made it happen, including advice for anyone looking to do the same.

Finding ways to get the fellowship accredited

Our Economics bachelor’s degree has a “Career Skills” program, a mandatory one-credit requirement that lets final-year Economics students choose from a number of pass/fail electives on a wide range of topics. We actually knew about this for a long time, but only thought to sign up much later. As far as we know, there is no official procedure for adding new courses, and we got in touch with someone at a different association who put us in contact with the program coordinator. So don’t be afraid to do some digging and just send an email stating your interest if you see a good fit for your fellowship somewhere.

We encourage you to look around for opportunities where the fellowship would be a good fit at your university. Some examples:

  • Career guidance programs (and career counseling programs)
  • Accredited professional courses (e.g., courses that teach specific skills such as Excel, programming, or foreign languages)
  • Faculty-specific courses (courses available only to economics/philosophy/history departments)
  • Electives

You can also just email the university and ask if they would be willing to accredit the fellowship as is (that is, validate the workload and acknowledge students’ effort) even if these credits do not count toward their degree.

First impressions

It is likely that a person (gatekeeper), or group of people, will be responsible for passing your request along before it’s officially considered by the university. That was our case. It is imperative that you make a good impression right away, which means preparing all relevant documents for your application before you begin presenting the course to anyone. These will depend on your situation, but you should be proactive and show that you’ve thought about the learning value of the course.

Here are the documents we prepared in advance for our initial pitch of the course:

  • Alignment of the course with our faculty’s learning goals (we had no idea what these were before this; we just got them off the internet). If you can find the learning goals of your specific degree program, even better.

  • The course workbook (including all the readings and exercises). Making it look pretty is easy and can significantly improve first impressions.

  • Breakdown of the workload. This was useful for us because the course had very specific workload requirements, but things might be different for you.

  • Optional: the assessment procedure. We did not have this at the beginning, but it probably helps. We would also include a statement of how your course fills a gap in the degree program. This can be either in the subjects it covers or in its methods (open-ended discussion rather than textbook learning).

Other things that can help you make a good impression:

  • Highlighting your previous experience running the fellowship. You can highlight your group’s experience with the fellowship. Successfully running the fellowship for multiple years with good participation and retention rates is a signal that the new course would just be business as usual and derisks the gatekeeper (e.g., the fellowship has been running twice a year for the past 3 years with an average of 15 students per cohort and a 75% retention rate).

We are still looking for a better-fitting name and are open to suggestions.

We do think that weaving EA concepts into established, professor-led courses might be even more effective, since a broader audience is reached for less effort from the group, though this depends heavily on how the professor frames EA. It goes without saying, but if you’re a professor at a university, establishing a course on effective altruism is a great way to share altruistic ideas with a large number of people at the same time (speaking as students ourselves, we would have killed to have such a course in our degree!).

We are unsure how the impact of an accredited course compares to the regular fellowship. In our situation, it’s likely that the accredited course is somewhat less impactful than usual. It’s plausible that offering credits means the students who join are less intrinsically motivated. We noticed that in the regular fellowship there was usually more consensus as people with opposing views self-selected out early. For us, the accredited course will be an addition to the regular fellowship, not a replacement for it.

  • We will invite more guest speakers next time. They bring expert knowledge that we can’t provide, and give students a direct, often more inspiring connection to people actually working in EA cause areas. We received feedback that our participants would have liked more speakers as well.
  • We will update the AI session with more up-to-date resources to account for the rapid pace of progress. We’d also like to partner with BlueDot Impact next time to sharpen how we communicate AI risk to Economics students new to the topic.
  • We will add cause-area-specific job content to the workbook, so students can see concretely what impactful work in economics-adjacent fields actually looks like.
  • We will do more targeted advertisements to increase the fit of people for the course.

Are you a group organizer?

If your group has been running the introductory fellowship for some time already, you should check if there are opportunities to get it accredited. We also had no clear avenue for it at first, so don’t be afraid to send some cold emails. It’s very low-cost, high-reward in terms of reputation, reach, and skill-building. item.title: Staying sane when the world isn't
item.description:
Published on November 13, 2026 6:00 PM GMT

This is a written version of a workshop I gave at EAG NYC in October 2026, edited to make sense in article form. Other materials: Slides with narrated audio, slides without audio, handout.

Introduction

"In war, what in ordinary times would be thought weirdly zealous becomes expected...For do-gooders, it is always wartime." - Strangers Drowning

I'm opening with this quote because I want to hold in mind that many people reading this are working under a mentality of high urgency.

The EA atmosphere has felt different to me since Hugging Face and the sea change in existential risk discourse. I know that for lots of us the times do not feel normal.

So this piece is about how to be more okay in abnormal times. It’s for anyone working under chronic urgency or moral demandingness - especially people working on x-risk, or anything else tethered to rapid advancements in AI. But in my experience the same themes apply to other cause areas too.

This isn’t about specific mental health problems, and I don’t assume readers have any. Instead I hope to persuade you that sanity and sustainability are nonnegotiables for all of us; to share some perspective from working as an EA therapist; and help you start planning for ongoing stability.

Where are you starting from?

Let's check where you're starting from. On the one hand, someone in a constant sprint at the edge of burnout who's doing nothing to care for themself should pause and sleep and probably make a plan for handoff.

But at the other end, sustainability isn't our only priority. At a certain point, adding more exercise (or fun, or rest) starts trading off against stuff we care about more.

So where we want to be is in the green, where we're putting our capacity to good use while also getting the full benefits of sustainability.

And my fear is that many of us enter the yellow too often - where we're working at a level that can't be sustained longterm, performing suboptimally, and constantly running a background risk of burnout.

The case for sustainability

The case for sustainability is simple. If you agree with three premises, working sustainably should be among your top priorities.

  1. We’re constrained. Humans are limited. We’re organisms. There are conditions where we function well, like being rested and calm; and those where we function poorly, like being distracted, exhausted, or stressed out for a long time.
  2. High-stakes problems need us at our best. The world’s most pressing problems are best attacked under conditions of not just adequate functioning, but excellent functioning. I'm thinking of things like creativity, clear reasoning, executive function, emotion regulation, and distress tolerance. These are really hard to do when you're unwell.
  3. The shortest timelines are longer than human cycles of burnout. People can burn out in weeks, and take their contribution to zero, faster than the window for contributing to our most important problems is closing. And it seems likely that the path to TAI routes through multiple points of high urgency, raising the costs of burning out too early. (Obviously, if you think I'm wrong here, feel free to continue sprinting unchecked - but I think that’s at risk of burning out and taking your contribution to zero.)

On valuing personal wellbeing

I’m aware the above framing is rather self-instrumentalizing. I don't want to debate how much weight to put on personal wellbeing for its own sake, mostly because similar actions are implied no matter where that lands.

But let me say this once clearly: I actively recommend you do stay in touch with the care you have for yourself, and with your preferences and desires, not just your basic needs.

This is not theoretical, and it's not a therapist platitude. I have seen people perform worse by their own lights because they instrumentalized themselves too hard. And I've seen that when people are able to re-enfranchise their own preferences and desires, it helps them persist more in important work. So please hear all of the recommendations here in the spirit of serving both worthy causes and personal wellbeing.

What does the literature say?

"...EAs seem to believe that work-life balance is a scam invented by Big Deontology to sell more low-impact charity.” - this post by ozymandias

That’s hilarious. Is there anything to it?

We can probably agree there exists a failure mode where people use concepts like work-life balance as cover for…doing whatever they want. But that is not the average calibration of people reading this.

And we’ll find that the research supports taking sustainability more seriously, not less. I'm deliberately keeping this part short, because you likely appreciates the bottom line already. But let’s briefly consider a few findings from contexts that have things in common with EA.

High-stakes professionals function better with rest

  • There's an extensive literature finding that doctors think less clearly and make more mistakes when they're working long shifts.[1][2]
    • And it's not surprising, given the effect of sleep deprivation: one study found that being awake for 24 hours degrades performance on a cognitive task as much as being drunk.[3] So if you face the choice of continuing to work at the end of a long day, recognize that's a decision to do your work impaired.
  • In the military, we see that people become less resilient to stress as the balance shifts in favor of more deployment and less rest.[4] But self-care, and working under leadership that prioritizes personal wellbeing, can buffer this a bit.[5]
    • If the literal armed forces can do self-care to stay mission-ready, so can you.
  • Among activists, people who feel like they can't rest are at higher risk of leaving the field.[6]

Psychological detachment is important

  • Another insight from the burnout literature is the idea of "psychological detachment" - having mental space that's totally unplugged from work.[7]
  • The research here shows that when you have headspace separate from work, you're less emotionally exhausted, better able to reengage the next day, and less likely to burn out when your job has a lot of demands.[8]

Conservation of resources theory

  • In organizational psychology, conservation of resources theory models stress and resilience in terms of people's resources.[9][10]
    • Resources are broadly defined here - not just things like money and health, but also goods like relationships or self-efficacy.
  • In this literature, losses and gains have asymmetrical effects of stress, just like loss aversion in behavioral economics. When you lose resources, you need a greater-than-equivalent gain to recover from that stress.
  • And often, you have to invest further resources to get that gain.
    • When you're socially isolated, you have to actively schedule time with people to restore a sense of connectedness.
    • If you're exhausted from being too busy, you have to purposefully protect and dedicate full nights of sleep to restore your cognitive performance.
  • The bottom line is that it's extremely important to avoid "loss spirals" - when your resources are depleted, you have less to invest to recover, so you're at risk of staying stuck.

On culture, briefly

  • If you run an org or manage a team, know that org-level interventions for burnout tend to do better than individual-level, at least in overworked physicians where most of this research is done.[11][12]
    • The types of things highlighted in meta-analyses are usually versions of decreasing demand on employees and increasing their agency.
  • We also know from the military that functioning well under stress requires unit cohesion.[13]
    • This is more than having friends and coworkers - it's a sense of shared mission, interdependence, cooperation and camaraderie.
  • But be careful that making the mission salient doesn't tip over into rewarding martyrdom, because that becomes a risk factor for attrition.[14]

Failure modes

I’m a therapist for EAs, and these are the most common errors I see people make in sanity and sustainability. Trust that I mean this section nonjudgmentally, as I’ve done all of these myself!

Assuming you need a complex solution

Or: "Not doing something obvious, because it sounds too obvious."

You might imagine someone who's struggling with productivity and distraction at work and thinks they need to go on medication or work with a coach. But really, the things they should check first are finding a more comfortable chair, or noise-cancelling headphones, or cleaning their room.

Discontinuing loadbearing practices when you're doing okay

If something is benefiting you, taking it away is a loss you’re likely to feel.

You might say, "Well, I don't want to have a bunch of unused capacity. If I'm sleeping 8 hours per night and have a bunch of important work to do, and I feel like I have plenty of energy, is it really so wrong to sleep 7?"

Maybe not. That's an empirical question. But whenever you remove a sustainability practice, consider that an experiment that incurs some risk, and be honest about what happens.

What about sprints? Sprints are fine if they are time-limited, for a specific high priority, you can afford to be temporarily depleted afterwards, and you have a plan for recovery. Many things we call sprints do not check all those boxes.

Not accepting tradeoffs (tactically)

It’s all too common that someone is excellent at thinking about tradeoffs abstractly, but then turns around and resists making them in practice. The error I usually see is someone just continues taking on new demands without checking what they're going to displace.

You cannot sum your effort to greater than 100%. So when you're considering a new project or commitment, actually ask, "What am I willing to trade away to make room for this?"

Not accepting tradeoffs (emotionally)

There’s also an emotional side of not accepting tradeoffs. Perhaps you realize you have to make them, but you’re also bemoaning this, and imagining how your idealized self could do everything, and recriminating yourself for not being higher-capacity. And that is a use of capacity.

You're allowed to grieve your human limits, but not constantly. You should spend most of your time just living by the math, within constraints.

The tyranny of infinite stakes

There's a phenomenon I noticed in clients with anxiety, especially OCD, long before I was working with EAs. The client would have a fear of something truly awful, like killing their own kid, and say effectively "I know I'm being irrational, but it would just be so bad." As if that settled the question of what to do. And then they would let the fear decide all of their next moves, including doing unhelpful compulsions and ruminating constantly, way past the point of actually serving the goal of keeping their kid safe.

I started calling this the tyranny of infinite stakes. It’s tyrannical because one consideration (how horrifying certain outcomes truly are) has unchecked power over all other considerations, including other top priorities (like their own sanity). And it even starts to obscure the practical question of how best to guard against the outcome.

EAs need to be wary of this tyranny because it plays into our disposition to think in terms of expected value. And when you put a term into the equation that's like, "This outcome is infinitely [bad/good] and therefore anything that feels in service of [avoiding/protecting] it is automatically the right call," the equation starts to break.

Spending down to zero

It's natural, if you're someone who's trying to maximize impact, to feel like as soon as a bit more capacity comes in, you should push it out the door in service of some important project.

But that puts you in a very high-risk and inflexible position. You always have almost-nothing in the tank.

So it's harder if you do need to sprint, and when stressors fluctuate you might run out of gas. You want to be able to go on work trips without getting sick every time. You want to be able to say yes to unexpected important meetings and crush them.

For more on spending down to zero, see this post.

Pain as the unit of effort

Speaking of good posts, "Pain is not the unit of Effort." It sure seems like we implicitly think it's virtuous to suffer as we do the good work. If you're not suffering, the view goes, you probably have more to give.

Well, I have many existence proofs that this is just not the case. People I know who are exceptionally productive in high-impact roles but just aren't miserable.

It's not just because they were blessed with a unicorn disposition so they can work constantly. The people I'm thinking of take vacations, and go dancing, and watch TV. And not even just because "this will let me work harder.” It's more like they have a picture of the good life that involves personal flourishing and rest, and also working super hard at times. Which is the portfolio I recommend.

At the end of the day, it's an empirical question whether people get better results when they're suffering or when they're flourishing. Don't be on the wrong side of it just because your social circles incorrectly valorize running yourself ragged.

If this resonates, I also recommend the Replacing Guilt series by Nate Soares, especially the post "detach the grim-o-meter."

Not asking for what you need

For folks who are probably more ask-culture than average, it's possible some of us need to go even further.

Maybe you can technically afford to volunteer your time, but you know you're at risk of feeling resentful if unpaid commitments pile up, so you ask whether there's funding. Maybe you're an evening chronotype, and you ask that your most important meetings don't get scheduled first thing.

"In abnormal times, normal things do not apply"

In some ways this entire workshop is trying to defeat this failure mode. But let's make it extremely explicit.

It is insane that AI might kill me, and you, and our children. Factory farming is insane, and biorisk, and infant mortality. The scale and stakes of these things are absolutely heart-exploding.

And. Absurd problems and abnormal times do not render everything absurd and abnormal. Some mundane laws of nature just keep on churning. Your body will continue needing sleep. You will still think less clearly when you're stressed and irritable. Your gut will continue to want things that feel joyful, no matter what your EV calculations say.

You can either see all of this clearly enough to account for the things that affect your ability to contribute; or not.

Anyone reading this has already passed through so many filters of moral luck, privilege, random chance and hard work to actually have a shot at personally helping with the problems you find most compelling. And even given that tremendous good fortune, some of us are gonna burn out. And some of those folks could have continued the good work if they had navigated differently.

So don't be fooled. Solving this world's deeply abnormal problems requires many normal things to go well beforehand. Your own stability is one of them that's most under your influence.

Underpricing normalcy

Closely related is underpricing normalcy in general. These nervous systems really like predictability. It takes a toll to be in constant threat-management.

So I strongly recommend you preserve access to "normal" spaces if you can - both social contexts and headspaces.

This is different that just not working all the time. It's spending time with people who don't think about x-risk. It's allowing your own brain to assume there will be a future even if part of you fears there won't.

I know it might feel like acting normal is one more cognitive bias we need to correct for, like we correct for scope insensitivity when making donations. But I think that's badly misguided. I've come to see normalcy as a sanity-preserving nutrient to protect, and I find that when I start to feel a bit too deep in AI substacks, letting my nervous system resettle in normal life for a bit helps me feel more grounded and stable, even when I turn back to EA topics.

Treating leaving as a fake option

No one actively claims that people can't leave things. But I find that the question of stopping, or quitting a job or taking a leave of absence, or leaving EA entirely, hits different when it's you. People treat it like it's correct to name it among one's options, but not correct to actually do it.

I won’t tell you what you should do. I happen to think it is allowed for people to leave. I think that if a situation is hurting you, it is right to look for an exit.

If you want to say it is tragic that people can't or don't push themself harder, that's fine.

But at least consider what effect it has on a person to tell themself they are trapped. We cannot have a culture that traps people.

For more in this direction, see this and this post.

#1 failure mode: Spending "work neurons" unstrategically

I saved this one for last, because it connects to the single most important technique I hope you take away from this article.

We've seen that being low-resource is a risk factor for burnout. And that in order to stay engaged longterm, you need to give your brain time away from work.

So it's no surprise that one of the least-helpful things you can do is spending attention in a way that gets you the worst of all worlds: Vaguely pointed in the direction of work so you're not getting a break, draining down your capacity, yet not actually moving projects forward.

Know when you're working and when you're not

In view of all this, my number one recommendation for people working under chronic urgency is as follows:

Know when you're working and when you're not.

(And switch modes fully and purposefully.)

Lessons from constructive worry time

This advice is inspired by one of my favorite CBT skills, "constructive worry time". It's an intervention for anxiety, when you block off time for deliberately thinking through unsolved problems, and otherwise you redirect your attention whenever you have an urge to ruminate, or else make a note to yourself that you can review during your next scheduled worry time.

Constructive worry time was developed as a corrective to people's default approach to worry, which is inefficient and burdensome. With worry, most of us tie up part of our attention on and off most of the time, in a way that gets all the costs of polluting your mood and attention but without getting the benefits of actually deliberate problem-solving.

My concern is that an analogous, unstrategic default happens in how people work in chronic urgency.

They feel some pull to think about work all the time, because it's so important.

But they do so unskillfully: 1) They end up less present for experiences that might otherwise be replenishing; 2) it prevents the psychological detachment that we know is protective against burnout; 3) and it's also not their best work - it's fragmented, repetitive and mindless.

So I think one of the most important things you can do is make your engagement in work more purposeful. 

Constructive worry vibes

You can certainly do the formal constructive worry time setup, where you schedule yourself time to think through all your extraneous work-related worries. The standard recommendation is usually half an hour a day toward the end of the day but not right before bed.

But I think it's even better if we also try to cultivate "constructive worry vibes" in how we allocate attention.

Here's what I mean.

  • Cultivate metacognitive awareness of where your attention is. You can do this by practicing mindfulness; by doing mental noting where you flag to yourself "I'm about to check Slack"; "I'm with my family but I'm thinking about a work project."; or even by talking to yourself out loud, "I'm pulling out my phone to look at AI Twitter."
  • Clean up your transition out of work. Identify in advance where you will pick up when you return, such as by making a to-do list for the next day. This reduces the urge to continue thinking about work. You’re able to say to your brain, "We are working the plan. I will get to that tomorrow at 8am."
  • When you have the urge to work more during personal time, pause. First ensure that 1) You endorse it for a specific reason, 2) You have capacity, and 3) It's not trading against something else important. Otherwise, schedule it for a time that's a better fit.

On doomscrolling

Here’s a corollary that’s almost too obvious to print: Be really careful about doomscrolling. It is way too easy to waste a bunch of neurons this way.

Instead, really try to make your media pay rent. When you're looking at work-related news or discourse, aspire to a bar where you can name what you're looking for, how you'll use it and why now is the correct time. No one has any reason to believe they're the exception to the attention economy. And because reading discourse from your field feels productive, you're probably miscalibrated on how worthwhile it is.

No free lunch

When you feel time constrained, it's natural to be drawn to things like "I'll just listen to this podcast on biosecurity while I'm folding laundry." As if it's a free life hack to be mentally working when getting something else done.

But the benefits of headspace away from work still apply, no matter what else also happened. Either it was good for you on net to have thought about pandemics for the additional hour that evening, or it wasn't.

Likewise, don't do brief dips in and out of work headspace if you can avoid it. It's not free to jump on x-risk twitter when you're going to the bathroom. That’s inviting attentional capture, making you less present for your life, paying the costs of attention switching; and all for brief, low-quality engagement.

To make these considerations vivid, try asking, "How would I design someone's lifestyle so they could never have a break from work?"

Maybe they could check their Slack before getting out of bed. Maybe eat all their meals at the office. Maybe only live with, date and hang out with people working on the same issues. You don't have to stop doing all these things; they might be worthwhile to you on net. But they are not free.

Make a sanity plan

In mental health it's common to make a safety plan for managing suicidality. The basic idea is to plan ahead for how you'll manage periods of acute risk, so that you don't have to do high-bandwidth problem-solving under especially bad conditions.

I recommend that you do something similar for sanity and sustainability. But unlike suicide safety plans which are mostly crisis-reactive, the sanity plan should be a balance of proactive and reactive. Here are the essential components I recommend for every sanity plan:

Physical self-care

In a powerful kind of therapy called dialectical behavior therapy, or DBT, taking care of your body physically is classified as an emotion regulation skill. That's for good reason: feeling well - strong, energetic, calm - makes everything else easier, including thinking clearly and managing stress.

You know this stuff. Actually do it.

Regular exercise pays for itself. Sleep pays for itself.

If you drink or use drugs more than you endorse, there is value sitting on the table every day you don't work on that.

And practice literally physically tuning in to how different habits make you feel below the neck. If caffeine makes you feel anxious and irritable, it's not performance-enhancing.

Mental health resources

I hope this one is self-explanatory. Mental health resources exist, including some culturally tailored to this community. Meds exist and make life more livable.

And please don't forget about emergency services if you're having thoughts of suicide or seriously hurting others:

  • US: Dial 988, text HOME to 741741
  • UK: Dial 999, Samaritans at 116 123
  • Go to an emergency room

Relatedly, as of Q4 2026, I'm currently trying to work out how psychologists can better support EA/AIS. If you have thoughts about resources your org or community could make use of, I'd love to hear that.

Social support

Social support, along with physical exercise, might be the intervention with the greatest consensus to make people more well.

If you feel chronically low on social support, see if you can think of one thing to do in the direction of getting more. It could be looking into a group or event, confiding in someone, or reaching out to someone you haven't been in touch with for a while.

Alternatively, if you have enough support yourself and some capacity to spare, consider if there’s someone in your orbit who could use some extra support.

Check-engine lights

Just like suicide safety plans, an important piece of a sanity plan is identifying: how will I notice that I need to make a change? Consider your own personal "check engine lights."

Most check-engine lights are some version of "I feel bad a lot of the time" (e.g. feeling chronically exhausted or tearful) or "I’m doing things I don’t endorse" (e.g. avoidance, withdrawing from friends).

"If…then" plans

In order for your check engine lights to mean anything, you should know what you'll do when they're going off.

It can be hard to predict what tradeoffs are justified in specific situations, but you can go ahead and pre-register some interventions that you endorse at least considering if things get worse in the future. Such as:

  • Looking into therapy
  • Starting or changing medications
  • Making a handoff plan for essential duties
  • Telling someone you need support
  • Reassessing after some sleep
  • Taking a leave of absence

I want to especially highlight making a handoff plan for essential duties. You don't want to end up in a position where you need to scale back at work for your own sanity (or maybe you just have the flu and need to rest) but you can't consider that because you're blocked on a belief that "I have too many responsibilities." Managers and chiefs of staff, you can do your part to normalize that planning for handoff for any high-stakes work is smart and normal.

(Also, I included “get some sleep” because mental health crises can be quite brief. Their peak acuity is often minutes to hours. So if you do find yourself in panic or despair, it is absolutely correct to get support, but I also hope you can take comfort that in the vast majority of cases, you will feel significantly better after some sleep, food and water and a change of scenery. So please don't make big or irreversible decisions at the height of emotion.)

Accountability

Tell someone about your sanity plan, or intentions you have for sustainability. Ideally this is someone who's close enough to you to notice when you need support, and whom you wouldn't mind hearing from if they're concerned about you.

Try to review your sanity plan regularly, both so it stays fresh in your mind and so you can update it if circumstances change. I recommend monthly or quarterly, and if you can tether it to something you already do like a quarterly review, even better.

Limits of all kinds

Consider limits on anything that, left unchecked, claims more of your capacity that you endorse. This may include:

  • Work hours: Is my schedule about right for me, trending toward too much, definitely way too much, or do I have room to comfortably work more?
  • Social media: For some of us, the move is “delete entirely.” Otherwise, you know about apps and blockers. If it's not working without them, it's silly not to try them.
  • Personal admin for issues of high urgency/demandingness: Many EAs are drawn to things like preparing your household for pandemics/infrastructure disruption, donation planning or morally auditing your budget. Give these block(s) of dedicated attention, but timebox them so you can mostly just live your life.
  • Discussion of work or x-risk during personal time (especially if you live with or are close with a lot of people in your field).

Not-to-do lists

Call to mind the sorts of things that tend to drain a lot of your capacity, lower your agency or generally jeopardize your mental health.

And then, when your capacity is especially low, consider a temporary ban on those things.

Maybe you have complicated family or a messy ex, and you're not interested in being estranged, but you know it's a bad idea to talk to them when you're in the middle of an important decision at work. Or maybe you commit to staying away from gambling or substances while you're trying to meet a deadline.

Choose your own sanity

Each of us have our own idiosyncratic ways of staying well and grounded, and these ought to be included in your sanity plan. Maybe it’s hobbies, socializing with non-EAs, religion, meditation, or reminding yourself of reasons we might not be doomed. It can be anything that's supportive of sanity and sustainability in your experience, as long as it doesn't have a bunch of downside risk.

Constructive grieving time

I like to say in therapy, only half-joking, "the rational response to life is to cry forever." One of the things I appreciate about EA is kinship with people who are appalled by the world's suffering and unwilling to normalize it.

But there's a cost to that. Being even somewhat in touch with the badness of the world’s worst problems, or the unboundedness and urgency of existential risk, is a heavy emotional weight to carry.

It's also a bit psychologically weird, in my experience, to be partly in touch with x-risk and partly just walking around getting groceries and chatting with neighbors. Even as I said before that normalcy is good for us, holding both sometimes leaves me feeling slightly alienated from part of myself.

So a handful of times I've found it helpful to set aside some time for neither engaging in EA, nor engaging in normalcy, but instead just to feel my own grief and fear and validate those feelings. I call this constructive grieving time, and it’s my own answer to “choose your own sanity.”

I do this in the form of a written conversation with myself, where I'll speak from the perspective of existential dread, or whatever emotion I feel drawn to attend to. Then I'll respond to it, as a kind of compassionate witness, offering validation or support. I just type this into a google doc like I'm writing a screenplay.

For me, a practice like this brings some emotional relief in the moment, and it also leaves me feeling freer in my headspace overall. That's why it's constructive - it gives your emotions proper attention, but it also gives that attention in a bounded way so most of your day can be spent living normally.

Next steps

If you're even a bit persuaded that there's something to all of this, here's what I recommend you do next. Right now, before closing this tab: make a calendar event, reminder or send yourself an email to say "Think more about sanity plan."

Then actually, literally fill out the sanity plan on the last page here. Fill it out now if you have time! Notice where there are gaps. Consider this your nudge to start therapy, meds, exercise or setting limits on overwork. Identify what needs to happen to patch your vulnerabilities.

And if you're in a position to do so, encourage people who might benefit from a sanity plan to make one.

May you be well

Thanks so much for giving some of your time to read this. And if you take any of the advice, I appreciate your trust, and your efforts to look after yourself. May you be well.
