Sequencing another ~1-2m clinical and community samples annually (including respiratory swabs and blood), using pooling where appropriate, may cost ~$50-100/sample, adding ~$50-200m/year. Additional spending on laboratories, rapid sample transport, bioinformatics, confirmatory sequencing, and reporting could bring the U.S. total to ~$200-500m/year. Expanding surveillance to international sites might bring the total to ~$1-5b, with room to grow. This relies on rough estimates from our Biosecurity & Pandemic Preparedness team.

  18. ^

    Gavi’s 2026-2030 budget of $11.9b came up $2.5b short at the 2025 replenishment (~$500m/year). Beyond Gavi’s current plans, CGD has also proposed a set of scaled-up interventions: a malaria vaccine catch-up for 45m under-3s plus every new birth cohort at $28/child; an HPV vaccine for 112.5m unvaccinated girls plus new cohorts at $10/child; and a rotavirus, pneumococcal, and typhoid package for 100m children at $24/child. Net of Gavi’s existing malaria and HPV plans, that comes to ~$3.4b/year. In addition, paying parents $2 per visit would help keep ~30m children born each year on the vaccine schedule, totaling ~$600m/year, focused on India, Indonesia, and Tanzania (where electronic vaccine registries allow quick scaling, reaching ~one-quarter of births in LMICs). The scale-up estimates take into account malaria (~10m) and HPV (~24m) vaccine coverage already planned in Gavi’s full replenishment ask.

  19. ^

    Some 270m people (~3% of the world) live outside mobile broadband coverage: ~180m have no mobile network at all, and ~90m have 2G only. Building ~82.5k new rural cell sites (assuming ~2k people served/site) at ~$145k each and upgrading ~40k 2G sites at ~$45k each, would cost ~$13.8b in capex, plus ~$1.6b/year to operate.

  20. ^

    There are no published estimates of the resources needed to bring to market a plant-based chicken breast product that has taste and price parity. Based on rough estimates from our Farm Animal Welfare team, $2b/year over 10 years could significantly increase the chances of this type of breakthrough. Funding would go toward R&D to take all major structuring routes to reduce costs, bring down ingredient costs, and test and iterate with consumers on products. Then, funding could be used for demonstration plants to test production at scale and providing commercialization support.

  21. ^

    We estimate that ~$1.5b a year in advocacy, over 30 years, would achieve stunning for ~50% of farmed fish. These are rough estimates from our Farm Animal Welfare team, extrapolating from the cost of fish welfare campaigns to date and assuming advocacy costs per fish helped rise as campaigns move to species where validated stunning methods don’t yet exist and which are not currently covered by aquaculture certification schemes.

  22. ^

    The Federal Aviation Administration’s aviation safety arm is ~0.7% of U.S. airline revenue, the Food and Drug Administration ~1.5% of U.S. prescription drug spending, and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission ~2.4% of U.S. nuclear generation revenue. Applying just the low end of that range (~0.7%) to the $130b combined annualized revenue of OpenAI and Anthropic gives $1b. The tens of millions for the spend of independent AI evaluators is a rough estimate using public funding announcements. It covers organizations focused on catastrophic risks, not the larger commercial market for general AI testing or companies’ in-house safety teams. This is based on rough estimates from our Navigating Transformative AI team.

  23. ^

    UNESCO estimates 262m in-school primary-age children fall below minimum reading proficiency. A catch-up for every non-reader would cost ~$2.6b one-off at $10/child, plus ~$600m/year to reach each new cohort, or only ~$800m/year over a decade.

  24. ^

    We estimate it would take further sustained advocacy, costing ~$750m/year for 30 years (~$23b), for 80% of hens worldwide to be permanently removed from cages. These are rough estimates from our Farm Animal Welfare team, extrapolating from the cost of cage-free campaigns to date and assuming advocacy costs per hen helped rise as a greater share of campaigning takes place in economies where retail and food service industries are more fragmented.

  25. ^

    For vaccines and cures, we use the WHO/Duke P2I model’s average costs and chances of success by product type and current stage, which gives the expected cost of getting one product approved: ~$2.2b each for a Strep A and a hepatitis C vaccine (nothing like them has been approved before, and both are in Phase 1), and ~$250m for a better hepatitis B cure (combinations are in Phase 2). A syphilis vaccine is further off, so we cost taking one candidate through early trials (~$90m), which comes to ~$4.8b. Alongside that, for syphilis testing and treatment today, which on its own can avert many deaths, we estimate technical assistance to procure tests, improve policies, and train health workers costs ~$0.60/birth, or ~$683m to cover the 120m+ births in all LMICs over 10 years. Together, that’s $550m/year.

  26. ^

    We estimate it would take ~$500m a year for 30 years (~$16b total) to ensure 80% of sows are no longer crated. These are rough estimates from our Farm Animal Welfare team, extrapolating from the cost of crate-free campaigns to date and assuming advocacy costs per sow helped rise as campaigns expand into countries where this advocacy is in its infancy.

  27. ^

    Our Navigating Transformative AI team estimated the cost of engineering necessary to research, develop, and produce solutions that can work at frontier scale, based on a “portfolio bets” approach that seeds many efforts in parallel. We expect to need teams with expertise in cryptography, frontier machine learning, formal verification, nation-state security, and AI accelerators and networking. There are a few problems to solve: allowing AI developers to declare their tasks so they can be privately checked for compliance; verifying with high security that the tasks were performed as declared, without revealing anything sensitive; and verifying that no undeclared tasks were covertly performed.

  28. ^

    The non-profit org Reflective has laid out a stage-gated research roadmap: existing evidence, small outdoor experiments, global distribution tests, monitored cooling. Their estimated cost is $370m-$1.36b, and they expect to take 10-22 years in total. We take the high end because running research in parallel to hit the fast timeline is the more expensive path.

  29. ^

    We estimate that, at a cost of ~$50m a year, 80% of male chicks worldwide can be spared. These are rough estimates from our Farm Animal Welfare team, extrapolating from the cost of technology refinement, industry outreach, and campaigns to date. This assumes advocacy costs per chick rise as adoption moves into less technologically developed markets.

  30. ^

    The total spend estimate (~$17.5b) reflects the sum of 2024 spending by Gavi, the Global Fund, the Gates Foundation, UNICEF (for child nutrition), major U.S. bilateral initiatives, and GiveWell in five areas — HIV (~$8.5b), vaccines (~$3.3b), malaria (~$2.6b), TB (~$1.9b), and nutrition (~$1.3b) — as recorded in IHME’s Development Assistance for Health database, plus for GiveWell its 2024 metrics, all converted to 2026 dollars, as described in this sheet. For lives saved, we divide the area total by the geometric mean of high and low estimates of cost-per-life-saved, as on this sheet, getting a total of 2.9m lives saved per year. The figures predate the 2025 aid cuts and exclude domestic and out-of-pocket spending. This is of course a very rough, illustrative model.

  31. ^

    This is based on each area’s global plan: WHO’s Global Technical Strategy for malaria, the Global Plan to End TB (as costed by Pretorius et al. 2023), UNAIDS’s Global AIDS Strategy (Stover et al. 2025), the Immunization Agenda 2030 (Sriudomporn et al. 2023; Carter et al. 2024), and the World Bank’s Investment Framework for Nutrition, and the math is in this spreadsheet.

  32. ^

    That is, we modeled the GiveWell opportunity set as isoelastic with eta = .375, implying that a doubling of expected funding should reduce marginal cost-effectiveness by 23% (1 – 2-.375 ≈ 23%). That was based on fitting isoelastic curves to projections GiveWell had performed, though they were very uncertain about those projections and wouldn’t want to independently defend them. Here, the estimates are in terms of cost per life saved for comparability with non-GiveWell-produced estimates.

  33. ^

    Our rough best guess of eta ≈ 0.65 comes from very roughly fitting a curve across health spending in the five areas above (HIV, malaria, TB, vaccines, nutrition), in three segments (current, the plans mentioned above, last-mile spending to 95% burden reduction). Under eta ≈ 0.65, each doubling cuts marginal cost-effectiveness by ~36% (1 – 2-.65). Eta ≈ 0.65 also roughly splits the difference with eta = 1, which we use as a conservative bound here and implies that doubling spending halves marginal cost-effectiveness. One caveat is that the 2021 fit was to GiveWell’s whole opportunity set, which values income gains plus lives saved; the marginal cost-effectiveness of that mix of outcomes should diminish more slowly than a curve that only looks at a narrower set of life-saving interventions.

  34. ^

    These are based on eta (from here using the actual letter η) = 0.375, 0.65, and 1, respectively. We model diminishing returns with an isoelastic curve: the cost, c, of saving an additional life rises with total spending, S, such that c(S) = c₀ · (S / S₀)η. If we raise spending from today’s ~$17.5b (S₀) to ~$54.5b (S₁) a year (adding the third wave’s ~$37b), and take ~$11,300 (c₀) as the approximate marginal cost now (roughly the cost per life of HIV spending, the most expensive area, in the underlying dataset), then lives saved = (S₀ / c₀) · [(S₁ / S₀)1-η – 1] / (1-η), or (S₀ / c₀) · ln(S₁ / S₀) when η = 1. That gives ~2.6m, ~2.2m, or ~1.8m additional lives a year, at each eta value.

item.title: RP needs $8M+ to further our work in GHD, cause prioritization, AI Strategy, neglected animal welfare, and more
item.description:
Published on November 16, 2026 4:47 PM GMT

TL;DR

  • We recently set out RP’s strategic priorities and the three new bets we’re making in 2027.
  • In this post, we outline what we need to make them happen.
    • We need more support from individual donors, this year in particular.
      • We’ve redirected roughly three-quarters of our 2026 unrestricted funding toward our new bets, and we no longer seek funding from EA-institutional grantmakers that may receive donations through our Cross-Cause Fund (to prevent any conflicts of interest).
      • Much of our work is also in frontier areas that institutional funders often can’t or won’t fund because of factors like scope limitations or risk aversion.
    • Two funding gaps are our highest priority, because they are very hard to fund through grants and so offer the best counterfactual value for your donation:
      • Next Priorities Funding ($4M): Unrestricted funding to uncover the next high-impact areas and interventions across causes, to move quickly on the most promising bets and to continue our work on the cross-cause model.
      • GHD Independent Research Funding ($350,000): Our most underfunded area: identifying strategic gaps and highly cost-effective interventions in global health.
    • Other key opportunities in need of support include: research on how transformative AI changes cause prioritization, a substantial update to the Moral Weight Project, our new AI Strategy Program and its project on the economics of transformative AI, the AI Cognition Institute, and our frontier animal work and Neglected Animals Project Fund.

 

You can donate here for unrestricted funding (highly encouraged). To donate to a concrete project, you can follow relevant links in the sections below. If you have questions, contact our development team or visit our donate page.

RP progress

Since its founding, Rethink Priorities (RP) has helped redirect millions of dollars in grants to more cost-effective global health options, produced welfare range estimates for animals that foundations and governments have begun using in their decision-making, coordinated ~$1.9 million from 14 funders for farmed animal welfare work across 16 EU countries, and brought farmed shrimp welfare to the attention of advocates and funders, inspiring the first organization dedicated solely to it. In 2026, RP advanced research on digital consciousness, AI in global health, and wild animal welfare. We also took a strategic lead in neglected animal welfare, launched the Cross-Cause Fund, helped 14 promising projects grow, and more.

Read about our key achievements this past year.

Our plans

2027 will likely continue to bring rapid advances in AI capabilities, creating both significant risks and major shifts across the areas EAs often care about. At the same time, more money entering the philanthropic space presents an exceptional opportunity to redirect resources and emerging initiatives to where they can do the most good.


Adapting too slowly to these circumstances may squander the EA movement’s chance for unprecedented impact.

In response, we plan to grow our core GHD, Animal Welfare, and Worldview Investigations teams to take on emerging priorities across causes. We’re also making 3 new strategic bets that we think will close crucial gaps in the EA ecosystem and help impact-focused philanthropists do more good than they otherwise would: 

  • Scaling the Cross-Cause Fund to $50M+ in donations, so the new philanthropic capital is allocated across causes through explicit, research-based modeling to maximize impact.
  • Launching an AI Strategy Program dedicated to identifying and acting on high-leverage, neglected strategies for navigating transformative AI (TAI).
  • Growing our Special Projects program to onboard 10 new initiatives a year, so promising initiatives and organizations can launch faster.

Read more about our 2027 strategy. 

We’ve made deliberate trade-offs to move these goals forward; now we need your support

RP always needs more support from individual donors. To this day, we have had the privilege of counting on the recurring support of a number of large, institutional funders. This kind of support can also be a structural limitation: our activities hinge on the financial health and strategic priorities of a handful of institutions. In addition, the bulk of our work is in neglected, frontier areas, where our goals often go beyond what institutional funders can or want to support.

This year, that need has become only more pressing. As laid out in our previous post, RP is building essential cause-prioritization infrastructure that the EA movement and broader charitable ecosystem urgently need to address the huge opportunities and challenges ahead. 

  • We’ve redirected resources internally toward our new strategic bets for 2027, spending approximately three-quarters of our 2026 unrestricted funding on these new opportunities and putting our Surveys and Data Analysis services on the back burner to free up staff time for these projects. The new programs we’ve launched are not self-sustaining: for example, we charge no management or usage fees for users of the Cross-Cause Fund and Donor Compass, which means we’re entirely dependent on other donors to maintain and improve these tools.
  • In accordance with our conflict of interest policy, we’ve also forgone seeking or receiving funding from all institutional grantmakers that may receive funds donated to our Cross-Cause Fund (including, but not limited to, The EA Animal Welfare Fund; The Navigation Fund’s Animal Welfare Fund; Longview Philanthropy's AI Fund). 

We’ve made these choices because we believe in the strategic bets we're making, and we want to give each of them the best chance of success we can. We've also taken steps to manage conflicts of interest because we believe they should be addressed responsibly and transparently.

This has left us with several funding gaps, both in our existing programmatic work and in our ability to further develop the new bets we’ve just launched. 

Our highest-priority funding gaps in 2027

Two areas need the most support this year:

  1. Much-needed priorities research for decision-making across causes through our Next Priorities Funding pool.
  2. Independent Global Health and Development research, through our dedicated funding pool – our most underfunded area.


Both are very hard to fund through grants, because grantmakers typically fund specific research programs rather than exploratory research. These projects will depend heavily on support from individual donors like you this year, so we think they offer especially high counterfactual value for your donation.
 

We are convinced some of the best interventions and approaches are yet to be uncovered. That’s why, with your help, we want to do bold research on what EA’s next priorities should be. 

Next Priorities Funding 

  • The gap: $4M of unrestricted funding to uncover the next high-impact areas or interventions, fast-track the most promising bets, and continue our cross-cause work.
  • The challenge: Few funders back research into new and cross-cause questions that nobody has looked into yet, which is where some of the greatest impact may lie. In a fast-shifting environment, one-off grants for narrow investigations may not keep up with the impact opportunities a broader approach can offer.
  • RP's plans: With Next Priorities Funding, RP can play its role as a bold priority-setter. We can take on complex, new and cross-cause topics where we suspect the greatest potential for impact lies, and move quickly when a promising bet emerges.
  • Why RP: RP has a track record of turning flexible, unrestricted funding into field-shaping work, including the Moral Weight Project and the Digital Consciousness Model.
  • Counterfactual value: You enable big bets that benefit entire fields to take off fast, rather than waiting for a funder to commission them.

Donate to Next Priorities Funding

GHD Independent Research Funding 

  • The gap: $350,000, equivalent to ~20% of the team’s time directed to independent research
  • The challenge: A lot of funding is expected to flow into global health and development, but there’s a risk that after saturating the most high-impact options, it will start moving to relatively lower-impact opportunities. We want to serve as a trusted, independent voice to uncover neglected areas in need of funding, and highlight existing interventions best positioned to absorb significant funds for maximum impact.
  • RP's plans: We already have an established list of priority areas and have started research in some of them, such as:
    • Identifying cost-effective opportunities at the intersection of traditional philanthropy and third-wave funds
    • Exploring how benchmarking affects model, product, user, and impact evaluations of AI tools deployed in global health and development (AI for Health, AI for Climate)
    • Tackling the growing burden of fungal diseases (global disease burden estimates)
    • Health Systems Strengthening
  • Why RP: Our comparative advantage is exposure to a wide range of GHD areas, and a team with diverse expertise spanning economics, epidemiology, and climate. We can spot gaps across whole fields as well as between interventions.
  • Counterfactual value: RP’s GHD department has historically relied on commissioned work to cover its budget, and our independent research in this area has been relatively underfunded compared to other cause areas. With more support, we can leverage our network and expertise to advance neglected, cost-effective interventions in this space.

Donate to the GHD Independent Research Funding

Other key opportunities in need of (additional) support

Your donation to these projects will help us build crucial additional capacity for teams faster than grants alone would allow. 

Note: The AI Strategy team will have a more detailed post on their strategy and their big bet idea later this week.

Transformative AI x Cause prioritization research

  • The gap: $500,000 to answer how transformative AI will change cause prioritization
  • The challenge: Transformative AI could reshape which causes matter most, how much they matter, and how soon. Yet these effects are barely understood, right as a new wave of philanthropy needs guidance on where to give.
  • RP's plans: Research how AI futures change the case for different causes, including economics, climate, and well-being effects, for example. We will use the findings in the model behind RP’s Cross-Cause Fund (CCF).
  • Why RP: RP and its Worldview Investigations Team (WIT) have a strong track record in this area. For example, the Moral Weight Project is used by several organizations, AI labs have looked at the Digital Consciousness Model, and the Cross-Cause Fund is likely the most rigorous tool for giving across causes. WIT has also newly recruited world-leading experts on these questions.

Counterfactual value: Few or no other groups do this type of work, and cause-specific grantmakers rarely fund it, so individual donors play an outsized role.

Donate to cause prioritization work 

Producing a substantial update to the Moral Weight Project

  • The gap: $400,000 to bring on more expertise to deliver rigorous, updated animal moral weights
  • The challenge: Funders working in animal (or AI) welfare need to know how to compare the welfare of different beings. The first version of the Moral Weight Project (conducted by RP between 2020 and 2022) provided the best estimates to date, but it rests on a single theory of welfare and covers a limited set of species. Several major animal grantmakers and organizations use this work and would benefit from updated and less theory-dependent figures.
  • RP's plans: First, we will map the range of approaches to estimating moral weights far more systematically and produce improved welfare estimates for 10 species from pigs to nematodes. We will also cover non-hedonist and theory-neutral approaches (e.g., ones that go beyond neuron counts). Second, we will develop methods for aggregating across theories, extend them to AI systems, and provide guidance on responsible use. The results will consist of robust, decision-relevant moral weights, showing which conclusions hold across approaches and which depend on assumptions.
  • Why RP: The first version of the Moral Weight Project is the most extensive attempt to estimate animal welfare ranges and is used by several organizations. The second version will build on existing work and in-house tools that have been developed since (Moral Parliament Tool, Digital Consciousness Model).
  • Counterfactual value: To our knowledge, no other group produces comparable moral weight estimates, so this work likely won’t happen without dedicated funding.

Donate to MWP
Please add a note “for the new Moral Weight Project” when you donate.

New AI Strategy Program: Building an all-in-one transformative AI strategy hub with advisory, fiscal sponsorship, incubation, and acceleration 

  • The gap: $750,000 toward helping the field spot neglected strategies for navigating transformative AI (TAI) and turn them into thriving projects and organizations
  • The challenge: The AI safety field lacks landscape-wide, regularly updated strategy research that any organization can use. In particular, new organizations in the field get too little strategic and operational support, and very little is currently available to help them scale.
  • RP's plans: We will take a two-pronged approach to fill these gaps: First, we’ll research and regularly update neglected, high-leverage strategies, and share them openly through a graphical strategy explorer. And second, we’ll expand incubation and acceleration, provide strategy advising, and launch new projects such as the project on the economics of TAI described below.
  • Why RP: Our Special Projects program has helped deploy $30M+ across 20+ projects, including Epoch AI, the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS), and Apollo Research.
  • Counterfactual value: We’re not aware of anyone else who offers field-wide, continuously updated, openly shared strategy research; no other AI safety fiscal sponsor or incubator offers strategy advising, and none combines fiscal sponsorship, incubation, and acceleration.

Donate to AI Strategy Program

Launching a project focused on independent economic analysis of TAI for policymakers

  • The gap: $250,000–$1,000,000 to launch a new project giving policymakers fast, independent economic analysis of TAI
    • $250K funds our first trial projects and core hires through mid-2027.
    • An additional $250K would fund a small policy desk for the full year.
    • An additional $250K–$500K, depending on funder interest, would also allow us to build up our measurement, deeper research, or field-building capability, as well as secure first-class senior advisors to help shape the project’s direction.
  • The challenge: Policymakers often make intrinsically economic decisions about TAI (such as how fast frontier AI should advance) without rigorous, nonpartisan economic analysis. Economics could also do much more research to help us understand how to reduce catastrophic AI risk, but this research is still in its early stages. Similar work, but for law and AI, has a dedicated institute (LawAI) focused on legal analysis for AI policy and broader fieldbuilding. Several academic centers research the economics of AI, but none seem to combine policy analysis with deeper research capability and a deliberate program to bring economists into work on TAI and its risks.
  • RP's plans: We will start as an independent desk producing fast, decision-ready analysis for policymakers. Our first study, on the economics of pacing frontier AI, will be published in the next month or two. With more funding, we’ll move into deeper economic research on reducing AI risk, measuring impacts of AI, extending our work to more jurisdictions, and broader fieldbuilding.
    • Why RP: This project came out of our landscape scan of around 170 strategies for navigating transformative AI. We build on RP’s track record of accelerating organizations such as IAPS, Epoch AI, and Apollo Research.
  • Counterfactual value: Your donation will let us run this trial project sooner, so we can test the hypotheses its theory of change rests on faster and have greater impact at a critical time in the technology’s trajectory. Institutional funders usually want to see results from trials like these before committing larger sums.

Donate to economic analysis of TAI

AI Cognition Institute (AICI): Additional research on assessing cognitive capabilities of advanced AI systems 

  • The gap: $500,000 to scale our rigorous empirical research on digital consciousness and the foundations of AI cognition
    • ~$400K for staff salaries; ~$100K for stakeholder engagement, including conferences, events, and mentoring
  • The challenge: AI consciousness and welfare research is pre-paradigmatic, with no shared framework for weighing the evidence. Few groups combine philosophical depth and empirical methods, inform key AI companies, and meet demand for this type of research, which is outpacing capacity.
  • RP's plans: We plan to produce an updated and shovel-ready Digital Consciousness Model (DCM) tool for AI companies in 2027, DCM forecasts of when future systems may cross precautionary thresholds, and an extension of the Moral Weight Project covering AI. We also plan to do direct mechanistic interpretability research on AI cognition and forecast the possible numbers of future digital minds. We want to develop a credible model of expert consensus for AI consciousness and welfare, and help to build a stronger talent pipeline.
  • Why RP: Our AICI team has active collaborations with several AI companies to utilize the DCM to evaluate model consciousness (including Google DeepMind), as well as Cambridge Digital Minds, PRISM, and the Center for Mind, Ethics, and Policy at NYU. We also have a strong candidate pool: in our last hiring round, seven applicants met our bar and we could only hire two.
  • Counterfactual value: Researchers and decision-makers seek answers in this space, but AI companies have said they won’t do this work in-house any time soon. We have funds to cover our baseline growth,  but flexible funds will let AICI hire and execute more ambitious projects sooner.

Donate to AI Cognition Institute

Scaling our frontier animal work

  • The gap: $500,000 to help fill key knowledge gaps and scale frontier animal projects across species, new fields, and talent programs
  • The challenge: Some of the biggest opportunities to help animals are in areas the animal welfare efforts have barely reached. Farmed insects, shrimp and fish, as well as wild animals make up the vast majority of animals affected by human activity, but the evidence needed to improve their welfare is largely nonexistent. Basic questions on interventions remain open, such as how to make electrical stunning reliably effective for farmed fish, or how to proceed responsibly in new fields like breeding for welfare. Without answers, advocates risk scaling interventions that don’t work, or missing those that would. These fields also lack skilled professionals and proven interventions, especially in neglected regions, and few other programs build capacity specifically for them.
  • RP's plans: Our 2027 research will aim to close key knowledge gaps and identify new opportunities, and our strategic guidance and coordination will help emerging areas start on solid ground and direct funding to resolving key bottlenecks. We will formally launch a Talent Program (successfully trialed in 2026) and kickstart a new Founders Program to bring skilled people and new projects into the areas of greatest need.
  • Why RP: Our frontier animal work builds on our track record of getting to areas like these early: we made significant progress on invertebrate welfare, launched and supported new organizations, and today play a coordination role in European fish welfare.
  • Counterfactual value: We already have institutional support for our core program, so additional donations would let us expand and accelerate this work, such as by supporting 2–3 more founders or talent associates, or resolving key welfare science questions more quickly. Our Cross-Cause Fund conflict-of-interest policy prevents us from seeking support for this work from two major animal welfare funders.  

Donate to frontier animal work
Please add a note “for frontier animal work” when you donate.

 

Neglected Animals Project Fund

  • A donation of any amount to enable early-stage, time-sensitive work and regranting for farmed insects and shrimp, and wild animals in 2027
  • The challenge: Some of the most counterfactually valuable opportunities for insects, shrimp, and wild animals are small, time-sensitive, early-stage projects that only happen when experts actively seek them out.
  • RP’s plans: RP Neglected Animals Project (NAP) Fund will support early, time-sensitive interventions in underexplored areas of animal advocacy to build welfare capacity and set precedents before harmful industry norms become entrenched. The work will include our own research and stakeholder coordination supporting new interventions and impact-focused organizations, as well as regranting, with most donations going to organizations and individuals starting or scaling welfare work in new industries and regions.
  • Why RP: Our neglected animals research expertise and close engagement with advocates help us identify promising opportunities and test their tractability before funding them. So far, the NAP Fund has helped us respond quickly to policy research needs, contribute to shaping a country’s national welfare guidelines for a commonly farmed and neglected species, and support the launch of new welfare work in several neglected, high-production regions. We can share more detail on the fund’s impact and plans with interested donors. Please get in touch at htookey@rethinkpriorities.org.
  • Counterfactual value: As major funders shift toward grants of $500K or more, these projects are increasingly likely to go unfunded or never start at all. Our Cross-Cause Fund conflict-of-interest policy also prevents us from seeking support for this work from two major animal welfare funders.

Donate to Neglected Animals Project Fund

Please add a note “for Neglected Animals Project Fund” when you donate.

How to give

Make your gift through the links listed in the sections above or go to our donation page for more options. We also encourage unrestricted donations directly to our Next Priorities Funding:

DONATE NOW

Donations to Rethink Priorities are tax-deductible in the United States and the United Kingdom. 

 

Under certain conditions, donations can also be tax-deductible in Canada, Germany, Switzerland, and the Netherlands. We also offer tailored support to determine tax-deductibility options in other countries. Contact us at development@rethinkpriorities.org, and we’ll advise you on your particular circumstances to maximize the impact of your donation.

Other ways to give

Donate through a DAF, donate stock through Every.org, or choose cryptocurrency. 

Get more information

If you have any questions, do not hesitate to reach out to our development team for more tailored support: 

  • Whitney Childs - Global Health and Development
  • Hannah Tookey - Animal Welfare
  • Janique Behman - All other areas
  • Kieran Greig - Wider organizational strategy and plans
  • development@rethinkpriorities.org - For general inquiries, technical questions, etc.

More ways you can help

We’re always looking for feedback on our work, as well as for new partners and potential hires. You can help us by:

  • Asking questions and raising disagreements about our work
  • Sharing our work and job opportunities with others
  • Making introductions to potential partners (for which you may email development@rethinkpriorities.org)

Thank you! 

Thank you for considering a donation to Rethink Priorities!

Your gift allows us to remain independent and to pursue the opportunities where we can have the greatest counterfactual impact.

By Marcus_A_Davis

Published on November 16, 2026 4:47 PM GMT

TL;DR

  • We recently set out RP’s strategic priorities and the three new bets we’re making in 2027.
  • In this post, we outline what we need to make them happen.
    • We need more support from individual donors, this year in particular.
      • We’ve redirected roughly three-quarters of our 2026 unrestricted funding toward our new bets, and we no longer seek funding from EA-institutional grantmakers that may receive donations through our Cross-Cause Fund (to prevent any conflicts of interest).
      • Much of our work is also in frontier areas that institutional funders often can’t or won’t fund because of factors like scope limitations or risk aversion.
    • Two funding gaps are our highest priority, because they are very hard to fund through grants and so offer the best counterfactual value for your donation:
      • Next Priorities Funding ($4M): Unrestricted funding to uncover the next high-impact areas and interventions across causes, to move quickly on the most promising bets and to continue our work on the cross-cause model.
      • GHD Independent Research Funding ($350,000): Our most underfunded area: identifying strategic gaps and highly cost-effective interventions in global health.
    • Other key opportunities in need of support include: research on how transformative AI changes cause prioritization, a substantial update to the Moral Weight Project, our new AI Strategy Program and its project on the economics of transformative AI, the AI Cognition Institute, and our frontier animal work and Neglected Animals Project Fund.

 

You can donate here for unrestricted funding (highly encouraged). To donate to a concrete project, you can follow relevant links in the sections below. If you have questions, contact our development team or visit our donate page.

RP progress

Since its founding, Rethink Priorities (RP) has helped redirect millions of dollars in grants to more cost-effective global health options, produced welfare range estimates for animals that foundations and governments have begun using in their decision-making, coordinated ~$1.9 million from 14 funders for farmed animal welfare work across 16 EU countries, and brought farmed shrimp welfare to the attention of advocates and funders, inspiring the first organization dedicated solely to it. In 2026, RP advanced research on digital consciousness, AI in global health, and wild animal welfare. We also took a strategic lead in neglected animal welfare, launched the Cross-Cause Fund, helped 14 promising projects grow, and more.

Read about our key achievements this past year.

Our plans

2027 will likely continue to bring rapid advances in AI capabilities, creating both significant risks and major shifts across the areas EAs often care about. At the same time, more money entering the philanthropic space presents an exceptional opportunity to redirect resources and emerging initiatives to where they can do the most good.


Adapting too slowly to these circumstances may squander the EA movement’s chance for unprecedented impact.

In response, we plan to grow our core GHD, Animal Welfare, and Worldview Investigations teams to take on emerging priorities across causes. We’re also making 3 new strategic bets that we think will close crucial gaps in the EA ecosystem and help impact-focused philanthropists do more good than they otherwise would: 

  • Scaling the Cross-Cause Fund to $50M+ in donations, so the new philanthropic capital is allocated across causes through explicit, research-based modeling to maximize impact.
  • Launching an AI Strategy Program dedicated to identifying and acting on high-leverage, neglected strategies for navigating transformative AI (TAI).
  • Growing our Special Projects program to onboard 10 new initiatives a year, so promising initiatives and organizations can launch faster.

Read more about our 2027 strategy. 

We’ve made deliberate trade-offs to move these goals forward; now we need your support

RP always needs more support from individual donors. To this day, we have had the privilege of counting on the recurring support of a number of large, institutional funders. This kind of support can also be a structural limitation: our activities hinge on the financial health and strategic priorities of a handful of institutions. In addition, the bulk of our work is in neglected, frontier areas, where our goals often go beyond what institutional funders can or want to support.

This year, that need has become only more pressing. As laid out in our previous post, RP is building essential cause-prioritization infrastructure that the EA movement and broader charitable ecosystem urgently need to address the huge opportunities and challenges ahead. 

  • We’ve redirected resources internally toward our new strategic bets for 2027, spending approximately three-quarters of our 2026 unrestricted funding on these new opportunities and putting our Surveys and Data Analysis services on the back burner to free up staff time for these projects. The new programs we’ve launched are not self-sustaining: for example, we charge no management or usage fees for users of the Cross-Cause Fund and Donor Compass, which means we’re entirely dependent on other donors to maintain and improve these tools.
  • In accordance with our conflict of interest policy, we’ve also forgone seeking or receiving funding from all institutional grantmakers that may receive funds donated to our Cross-Cause Fund (including, but not limited to, The EA Animal Welfare Fund; The Navigation Fund’s Animal Welfare Fund; Longview Philanthropy's AI Fund). 

We’ve made these choices because we believe in the strategic bets we're making, and we want to give each of them the best chance of success we can. We've also taken steps to manage conflicts of interest because we believe they should be addressed responsibly and transparently.

This has left us with several funding gaps, both in our existing programmatic work and in our ability to further develop the new bets we’ve just launched. 

Our highest-priority funding gaps in 2027

Two areas need the most support this year:

  1. Much-needed priorities research for decision-making across causes through our Next Priorities Funding pool.
  2. Independent Global Health and Development research, through our dedicated funding pool – our most underfunded area.


Both are very hard to fund through grants, because grantmakers typically fund specific research programs rather than exploratory research. These projects will depend heavily on support from individual donors like you this year, so we think they offer especially high counterfactual value for your donation.
 

We are convinced some of the best interventions and approaches are yet to be uncovered. That’s why, with your help, we want to do bold research on what EA’s next priorities should be. 

Next Priorities Funding 

  • The gap: $4M of unrestricted funding to uncover the next high-impact areas or interventions, fast-track the most promising bets, and continue our cross-cause work.
  • The challenge: Few funders back research into new and cross-cause questions that nobody has looked into yet, which is where some of the greatest impact may lie. In a fast-shifting environment, one-off grants for narrow investigations may not keep up with the impact opportunities a broader approach can offer.
  • RP's plans: With Next Priorities Funding, RP can play its role as a bold priority-setter. We can take on complex, new and cross-cause topics where we suspect the greatest potential for impact lies, and move quickly when a promising bet emerges.
  • Why RP: RP has a track record of turning flexible, unrestricted funding into field-shaping work, including the Moral Weight Project and the Digital Consciousness Model.
  • Counterfactual value: You enable big bets that benefit entire fields to take off fast, rather than waiting for a funder to commission them.

Donate to Next Priorities Funding

GHD Independent Research Funding 

  • The gap: $350,000, equivalent to ~20% of the team’s time directed to independent research
  • The challenge: A lot of funding is expected to flow into global health and development, but there’s a risk that after saturating the most high-impact options, it will start moving to relatively lower-impact opportunities. We want to serve as a trusted, independent voice to uncover neglected areas in need of funding, and highlight existing interventions best positioned to absorb significant funds for maximum impact.
  • RP's plans: We already have an established list of priority areas and have started research in some of them, such as:
    • Identifying cost-effective opportunities at the intersection of traditional philanthropy and third-wave funds
    • Exploring how benchmarking affects model, product, user, and impact evaluations of AI tools deployed in global health and development (AI for Health, AI for Climate)
    • Tackling the growing burden of fungal diseases (global disease burden estimates)
    • Health Systems Strengthening
  • Why RP: Our comparative advantage is exposure to a wide range of GHD areas, and a team with diverse expertise spanning economics, epidemiology, and climate. We can spot gaps across whole fields as well as between interventions.
  • Counterfactual value: RP’s GHD department has historically relied on commissioned work to cover its budget, and our independent research in this area has been relatively underfunded compared to other cause areas. With more support, we can leverage our network and expertise to advance neglected, cost-effective interventions in this space.

Donate to the GHD Independent Research Funding

Other key opportunities in need of (additional) support

Your donation to these projects will help us build crucial additional capacity for teams faster than grants alone would allow. 

Note: The AI Strategy team will have a more detailed post on their strategy and their big bet idea later this week.

Transformative AI x Cause prioritization research

  • The gap: $500,000 to answer how transformative AI will change cause prioritization
  • The challenge: Transformative AI could reshape which causes matter most, how much they matter, and how soon. Yet these effects are barely understood, right as a new wave of philanthropy needs guidance on where to give.
  • RP's plans: Research how AI futures change the case for different causes, including economics, climate, and well-being effects, for example. We will use the findings in the model behind RP’s Cross-Cause Fund (CCF).
  • Why RP: RP and its Worldview Investigations Team (WIT) have a strong track record in this area. For example, the Moral Weight Project is used by several organizations, AI labs have looked at the Digital Consciousness Model, and the Cross-Cause Fund is likely the most rigorous tool for giving across causes. WIT has also newly recruited world-leading experts on these questions.

Counterfactual value: Few or no other groups do this type of work, and cause-specific grantmakers rarely fund it, so individual donors play an outsized role.

Donate to cause prioritization work 

Producing a substantial update to the Moral Weight Project

  • The gap: $400,000 to bring on more expertise to deliver rigorous, updated animal moral weights
  • The challenge: Funders working in animal (or AI) welfare need to know how to compare the welfare of different beings. The first version of the Moral Weight Project (conducted by RP between 2020 and 2022) provided the best estimates to date, but it rests on a single theory of welfare and covers a limited set of species. Several major animal grantmakers and organizations use this work and would benefit from updated and less theory-dependent figures.
  • RP's plans: First, we will map the range of approaches to estimating moral weights far more systematically and produce improved welfare estimates for 10 species from pigs to nematodes. We will also cover non-hedonist and theory-neutral approaches (e.g., ones that go beyond neuron counts). Second, we will develop methods for aggregating across theories, extend them to AI systems, and provide guidance on responsible use. The results will consist of robust, decision-relevant moral weights, showing which conclusions hold across approaches and which depend on assumptions.
  • Why RP: The first version of the Moral Weight Project is the most extensive attempt to estimate animal welfare ranges and is used by several organizations. The second version will build on existing work and in-house tools that have been developed since (Moral Parliament Tool, Digital Consciousness Model).
  • Counterfactual value: To our knowledge, no other group produces comparable moral weight estimates, so this work likely won’t happen without dedicated funding.

Donate to MWP
Please add a note “for the new Moral Weight Project” when you donate.

New AI Strategy Program: Building an all-in-one transformative AI strategy hub with advisory, fiscal sponsorship, incubation, and acceleration 

  • The gap: $750,000 toward helping the field spot neglected strategies for navigating transformative AI (TAI) and turn them into thriving projects and organizations
  • The challenge: The AI safety field lacks landscape-wide, regularly updated strategy research that any organization can use. In particular, new organizations in the field get too little strategic and operational support, and very little is currently available to help them scale.
  • RP's plans: We will take a two-pronged approach to fill these gaps: First, we’ll research and regularly update neglected, high-leverage strategies, and share them openly through a graphical strategy explorer. And second, we’ll expand incubation and acceleration, provide strategy advising, and launch new projects such as the project on the economics of TAI described below.
  • Why RP: Our Special Projects program has helped deploy $30M+ across 20+ projects, including Epoch AI, the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS), and Apollo Research.
  • Counterfactual value: We’re not aware of anyone else who offers field-wide, continuously updated, openly shared strategy research; no other AI safety fiscal sponsor or incubator offers strategy advising, and none combines fiscal sponsorship, incubation, and acceleration.

Donate to AI Strategy Program

Launching a project focused on independent economic analysis of TAI for policymakers

  • The gap: $250,000–$1,000,000 to launch a new project giving policymakers fast, independent economic analysis of TAI
    • $250K funds our first trial projects and core hires through mid-2027.
    • An additional $250K would fund a small policy desk for the full year.
    • An additional $250K–$500K, depending on funder interest, would also allow us to build up our measurement, deeper research, or field-building capability, as well as secure first-class senior advisors to help shape the project’s direction.
  • The challenge: Policymakers often make intrinsically economic decisions about TAI (such as how fast frontier AI should advance) without rigorous, nonpartisan economic analysis. Economics could also do much more research to help us understand how to reduce catastrophic AI risk, but this research is still in its early stages. Similar work, but for law and AI, has a dedicated institute (LawAI) focused on legal analysis for AI policy and broader fieldbuilding. Several academic centers research the economics of AI, but none seem to combine policy analysis with deeper research capability and a deliberate program to bring economists into work on TAI and its risks.
  • RP's plans: We will start as an independent desk producing fast, decision-ready analysis for policymakers. Our first study, on the economics of pacing frontier AI, will be published in the next month or two. With more funding, we’ll move into deeper economic research on reducing AI risk, measuring impacts of AI, extending our work to more jurisdictions, and broader fieldbuilding.
    • Why RP: This project came out of our landscape scan of around 170 strategies for navigating transformative AI. We build on RP’s track record of accelerating organizations such as IAPS, Epoch AI, and Apollo Research.
  • Counterfactual value: Your donation will let us run this trial project sooner, so we can test the hypotheses its theory of change rests on faster and have greater impact at a critical time in the technology’s trajectory. Institutional funders usually want to see results from trials like these before committing larger sums.

Donate to economic analysis of TAI

AI Cognition Institute (AICI): Additional research on assessing cognitive capabilities of advanced AI systems 

  • The gap: $500,000 to scale our rigorous empirical research on digital consciousness and the foundations of AI cognition
    • ~$400K for staff salaries; ~$100K for stakeholder engagement, including conferences, events, and mentoring
  • The challenge: AI consciousness and welfare research is pre-paradigmatic, with no shared framework for weighing the evidence. Few groups combine philosophical depth and empirical methods, inform key AI companies, and meet demand for this type of research, which is outpacing capacity.
  • RP's plans: We plan to produce an updated and shovel-ready Digital Consciousness Model (DCM) tool for AI companies in 2027, DCM forecasts of when future systems may cross precautionary thresholds, and an extension of the Moral Weight Project covering AI. We also plan to do direct mechanistic interpretability research on AI cognition and forecast the possible numbers of future digital minds. We want to develop a credible model of expert consensus for AI consciousness and welfare, and help to build a stronger talent pipeline.
  • Why RP: Our AICI team has active collaborations with several AI companies to utilize the DCM to evaluate model consciousness (including Google DeepMind), as well as Cambridge Digital Minds, PRISM, and the Center for Mind, Ethics, and Policy at NYU. We also have a strong candidate pool: in our last hiring round, seven applicants met our bar and we could only hire two.
  • Counterfactual value: Researchers and decision-makers seek answers in this space, but AI companies have said they won’t do this work in-house any time soon. We have funds to cover our baseline growth,  but flexible funds will let AICI hire and execute more ambitious projects sooner.

Donate to AI Cognition Institute

Scaling our frontier animal work

  • The gap: $500,000 to help fill key knowledge gaps and scale frontier animal projects across species, new fields, and talent programs
  • The challenge: Some of the biggest opportunities to help animals are in areas the animal welfare efforts have barely reached. Farmed insects, shrimp and fish, as well as wild animals make up the vast majority of animals affected by human activity, but the evidence needed to improve their welfare is largely nonexistent. Basic questions on interventions remain open, such as how to make electrical stunning reliably effective for farmed fish, or how to proceed responsibly in new fields like breeding for welfare. Without answers, advocates risk scaling interventions that don’t work, or missing those that would. These fields also lack skilled professionals and proven interventions, especially in neglected regions, and few other programs build capacity specifically for them.
  • RP's plans: Our 2027 research will aim to close key knowledge gaps and identify new opportunities, and our strategic guidance and coordination will help emerging areas start on solid ground and direct funding to resolving key bottlenecks. We will formally launch a Talent Program (successfully trialed in 2026) and kickstart a new Founders Program to bring skilled people and new projects into the areas of greatest need.
  • Why RP: Our frontier animal work builds on our track record of getting to areas like these early: we made significant progress on invertebrate welfare, launched and supported new organizations, and today play a coordination role in European fish welfare.
  • Counterfactual value: We already have institutional support for our core program, so additional donations would let us expand and accelerate this work, such as by supporting 2–3 more founders or talent associates, or resolving key welfare science questions more quickly. Our Cross-Cause Fund conflict-of-interest policy prevents us from seeking support for this work from two major animal welfare funders.  

Donate to frontier animal work
Please add a note “for frontier animal work” when you donate.

 

Neglected Animals Project Fund

  • A donation of any amount to enable early-stage, time-sensitive work and regranting for farmed insects and shrimp, and wild animals in 2027
  • The challenge: Some of the most counterfactually valuable opportunities for insects, shrimp, and wild animals are small, time-sensitive, early-stage projects that only happen when experts actively seek them out.
  • RP’s plans: RP Neglected Animals Project (NAP) Fund will support early, time-sensitive interventions in underexplored areas of animal advocacy to build welfare capacity and set precedents before harmful industry norms become entrenched. The work will include our own research and stakeholder coordination supporting new interventions and impact-focused organizations, as well as regranting, with most donations going to organizations and individuals starting or scaling welfare work in new industries and regions.
  • Why RP: Our neglected animals research expertise and close engagement with advocates help us identify promising opportunities and test their tractability before funding them. So far, the NAP Fund has helped us respond quickly to policy research needs, contribute to shaping a country’s national welfare guidelines for a commonly farmed and neglected species, and support the launch of new welfare work in several neglected, high-production regions. We can share more detail on the fund’s impact and plans with interested donors. Please get in touch at htookey@rethinkpriorities.org.
  • Counterfactual value: As major funders shift toward grants of $500K or more, these projects are increasingly likely to go unfunded or never start at all. Our Cross-Cause Fund conflict-of-interest policy also prevents us from seeking support for this work from two major animal welfare funders.

item.title: The Boy Who Stole Billions: what the first two episodes show about effective altruism and earning to give
item.description:
Published on November 17, 2026 12:20 AM GMT

I watched the first two episodes of The Boy Who Stole Billions, an upcoming Amazon series directed by Nanette Burstein about the convicted fraudster Sam Bankman-Fried, shown as a world premiere at DOC NYC.

In 2022, during the FTX scandal, I had never heard of effective altruism, and I barely remember the scandal itself. Today I encourage people to use EA principles for their careers and their giving, so I regularly get questions about it. The first impressions below are my own; the full summary of the two episodes was mostly written with AI. I’m writing in a personal capacity.

This post doesn’t aim to impose a reading of the series, and it isn’t a guide to answering questions on the topic. For that, the Centre for Effective Altruism’s post by @Tess Newton-Palmer on how to talk about the other FTX series, Netflix’s The Altruists (quite a month for TV shows on this topic) may be more useful for you. 


TL;DR: Effective altruism is at the heart of most of the first episode. The series seems to aim at reflecting reality without painting a very negative picture of EA. It shows that earning to give is what led Sam into this sector, and also that some of the effective altruists who worked with him early on, Tara Mac Aulay in particular, pushed for more prudence and for keeping promises to investors. Over the first two episodes, Sam comes across increasingly as a gambler, more and more detached from his initial altruistic goals.

What I took from the episodes: the gambler and the EAs who pushed back

The series presents Sam as a utilitarian loner and gambler inspired by earning to give, but it also lets other voices inspired by effective altruism be heard.

Earning to give at the root of the story

My view is that the series doesn’t stray far from reality. Even though effective altruism is mostly seen through the lens of earning to give, it is directly what led Sam into this sector. The documentary leans quite heavily on EA, with several excerpts from EA conference talks, notably by Will MacAskill, whose role in Sam’s path is well documented.

There is also the testimony of Tara Mac Aulay, former CEO of the Centre for Effective Altruism and co-founder of Alameda Research. Even though she helped Sam get into crypto and co-founded the company with him, I’d say she represents effective altruism well, because she is clearly one of the sane and ethical people featured in the documentary. She explains the disagreements over risk management and business ethics, and what led her to leave.

The documentary doesn’t paint the worst possible picture of SBF (I was surprised by some of the choices, which, to me, cast a somewhat a neutral, or even somewhat positive, light on someone who committed such a massive fraud). It begins with his childhood and includes testimony from his parents. Sam also describes his anhedonia, his inability to feel pleasure or joy. It also builds a narrative of Sam as a very isolated person who makes extremely dangerous decisions.

The early EAs depicted as the voice of reason

Some members of the EA community worked for Sam in the early days. They didn’t support his decisions and tried to oppose him and slow him down: take fewer risks, test before launching, don’t break promises to investors. When decisions became far too dangerous, they judged that this was not acceptable and chose to leave. Tara and others gave Sam an ultimatum, he refused, and around half the company left. This part relies mostly on Tara’s account, and Sam gets to give his side.

So in this first episode, members of the EA community are both the people who said “making a lot of money to give it away is good” and the people who tried to bring back reason and a careful use of funds.

The series also shows that, as Sam became famous, the community put him on a pedestal, even though, according to Tara, Alameda had made no donations during her time there. She says Sam warned her that the community would believe his version over hers. She describes feeling vulnerable after leaving, with her place in the EA community and her whole social life at stake, and starting to doubt herself as the community held him up as a model.

Altruistic motivations, then a drift

As the series tells it, the initial motivations are clear: these are very altruistic people, Sam included. Around him are people who want to have a positive impact: Tara; Wayne Hsiung, an animal rights activist active on the EA Forum, who pushed back against earning to give; and later Nishad Singh, an early Alameda employee who went on to head engineering at FTX, who complains that they still haven’t started giving.

After the split, the company turns more and more towards people willing to take risks. Most of the new hires were not looking to have an impact; they just wanted to get rich. While the first people involved were, perhaps, altruists, FTX became a money-maximising operation.

Sam keeps reasoning in terms of expected value, for instance arguing that a 20% chance of FTX not being a flop is enough to justify it. Yet none of the people depicted as effective altruists in the series makes this kind of argument, and by then most of the early ones have left. In a way, they come across as the voice of reason. Through Tara’s voice, effective altruism is associated with prudence and with the importance of keeping promises and not deceiving people.

Over the two episodes, Sam goes further and further in pursuit of more money, more profit, without starting to give significantly, and seems more and more detached from any altruistic goal. My personal impression is of a gambler going double or nothing every three months; what the series shows is Sam’s growing delusions of grandeur. The series also points out how little was donated compared with the company’s valuation, criticises the investment in a coal-powered mine on climate grounds, and shows the money spent on advertising. In the show’s narrative, all of this seems tied to the delusions of grandeur Sam develops as the episodes go on.

The relationship with Caroline

His relationship with Caroline Ellison is at the heart of the second episode. The episode ends with the first signs of trouble in Alameda’s management: the firm relies mostly on its own assets, which are far too unstable.

Summary of episodes 1 and 2

This summary of the two episodes was mostly written with AI.

Episode 1: from effective altruism to Alameda

The episode opens at the FTX Crypto Bahamas conference, with celebrities and former world leaders on stage, then cuts to the collapse: Sam Bankman-Fried was found guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy, about $8 billion of customer money is gone, and victims describe their losses. Sam takes part in the series through video calls from federal prison, limited to about 15 minutes a day. He says he wants “to get the truth out there”, even though the truth “has not been kind” to him.

Childhood and early ideas. Sam grows up near Stanford, where both his parents teach law. His parents describe a quiet, introverted child who didn’t fit in and responded to logic more than emotion. At a summer maths camp he meets Sam Trabucco and Gary Wang, who both play a role later. Trabucco remembers a teenager already talking about utilitarianism and expected value.

Discovering effective altruism. As a student at MIT, Sam finds the early EA community through an online forum and feels, for the first time, that he is not alone. Tara Mac Aulay explains the basic ideas: give 10% of your income and find the charities that do the most good per dollar. The series includes archive footage from EA talks, including a debate in which Will MacAskill says that, between saving a child or a Picasso from a burning building, he would save the Picasso and sell it to save many more children. Sam is drawn above all to animal welfare. Wayne Hsiung, an animal rights activist, remembers a young man who cared about neither wealth nor status. Will MacAskill suggests earning to give in finance. Hsiung thinks this would be a waste, but Sam follows MacAskill’s advice: he sees himself as bad at outreach and good at maths.

Jane Street. Sam joins Jane Street, a top trading firm where trading feels like a game. He donates six figures a year, feels no joy, and after an EA conference starts asking whether he could do more good elsewhere. With Tara, then CEO of the Centre for Effective Altruism, he maps out his options on a whiteboard. Tara shows him large price gaps for Bitcoin between exchanges. Sam, sceptical of crypto at first, realises it could be a huge trading opportunity and leaves Jane Street.

Founding Alameda Research. Sam and Tara found Alameda Research in 2017. All the equity is put in Sam’s name. Tara accepts because, as EAs, they plan to donate all profits anyway. Gary Wang builds the trading software, the team lives and works in a chaotic house in Berkeley, and investors from the EA community lend between $1 million and $100 million each, with a high level of trust because the profits are meant for charity. Nishad Singh, an EA and vegan who wanted to earn to give, joins; his wife describes his ambition and kindness. A trade between Japanese and US Bitcoin prices brings in around a million dollars a day. Tara explains that when a few thousand dollars can save a life, it becomes very hard to stop working.

Crisis and split. In early 2018 the crypto market crashes and wipes out most of the profits. Tara worked herself into the hospital. Around $15 million of crypto appears to be missing; Sam says later it was an accounting error and was recovered. The key conflict concerns a new trading bot: Tara wants it tested first, Sam agrees at a meeting with the lenders not to launch it untested, then switches it on the next day. Tara sees this as breaking a promise that put the investors’ money at risk. She also links Sam’s appetite for risk to his anhedonia, his inability to feel pleasure or joy, which he describes himself. Tara and part of the team try to buy him out and give him an ultimatum. He refuses, declares them fired, and about half the company leaves.

Sam loses most of his friends and roommates. He notes that the wider EA community took no formal position on who was right. Tara says Sam made clear that, as a rich, well-connected white man, his version would be believed over hers. She felt her place in the community, and her whole social life, were at risk. As Sam becomes a media figure, she starts to doubt herself, especially as the EA community holds him up as a model, although Alameda had made no donations while she was there. Archive footage shows MacAskill citing Sam’s success as proof that people can aim for even greater impact.

Episode 2: the relationship with Caroline and the rise of FTX

Hong Kong and new hires. Sam says he wanted to put distance between himself and the EA community to avoid a wider split, and moves Alameda to Hong Kong, then the centre of the crypto world. He recruits Sam Trabucco, who was not into effective altruism and wanted to get rich. Trabucco explains that the EAs who left were uncomfortable with almost any risk, and Sam wanted experienced traders. Caroline Ellison, a former Jane Street trader who shares Sam’s maths and EA background, also joins. Trabucco and Caroline soon run Alameda together. Sam and Caroline begin a relationship, largely through long written exchanges, which Sam insists on keeping secret.

Founding FTX. Sam decides to build a crypto exchange because exchanges earn fees on every trade. He reasons that a 20% chance of it not being a flop is enough to justify the bet. I watched the first two episodes of The Boy Who Stole Billions, an upcoming Amazon series directed by Nanette Burstein about the convicted fraudster Sam Bankman-Fried, shown as a world premiere at DOC NYC.

In 2022, during the FTX scandal, I had never heard of effective altruism, and I barely remember the scandal itself. Today I encourage people to use EA principles for their careers and their giving, so I regularly get questions about it. The first impressions below are my own; the full summary of the two episodes was mostly written with AI. I’m writing in a personal capacity.

This post doesn’t aim to impose a reading of the series, and it isn’t a guide to answering questions on the topic. For that, the Centre for Effective Altruism’s post by @Tess Newton-Palmer on how to talk about the other FTX series, Netflix’s The Altruists (quite a month for TV shows on this topic) may be more useful for you. 


TL;DR: Effective altruism is at the heart of most of the first episode. The series seems to aim at reflecting reality without painting a very negative picture of EA. It shows that earning to give is what led Sam into this sector, and also that some of the effective altruists who worked with him early on, Tara Mac Aulay in particular, pushed for more prudence and for keeping promises to investors. Over the first two episodes, Sam comes across increasingly as a gambler, more and more detached from his initial altruistic goals.

What I took from the episodes: the gambler and the EAs who pushed back

The series presents Sam as a utilitarian loner and gambler inspired by earning to give, but it also lets other voices inspired by effective altruism be heard.

Earning to give at the root of the story

My view is that the series doesn’t stray far from reality. Even though effective altruism is mostly seen through the lens of earning to give, it is directly what led Sam into this sector. The documentary leans quite heavily on EA, with several excerpts from EA conference talks, notably by Will MacAskill, whose role in Sam’s path is well documented.

There is also the testimony of Tara Mac Aulay, former CEO of the Centre for Effective Altruism and co-founder of Alameda Research. Even though she helped Sam get into crypto and co-founded the company with him, I’d say she represents effective altruism well, because she is clearly one of the sane and ethical people featured in the documentary. She explains the disagreements over risk management and business ethics, and what led her to leave.

The documentary doesn’t paint the worst possible picture of SBF (I was surprised by some of the choices, which, to me, cast a somewhat a neutral, or even somewhat positive, light on someone who committed such a massive fraud). It begins with his childhood and includes testimony from his parents. Sam also describes his anhedonia, his inability to feel pleasure or joy. It also builds a narrative of Sam as a very isolated person who makes extremely dangerous decisions.

Some members of the EA community worked for Sam in the early days. They didn’t support his decisions and tried to oppose him and slow him down: take fewer risks, test before launching, don’t break promises to investors. When decisions became far too dangerous, they judged that this was not acceptable and chose to leave. Tara and others gave Sam an ultimatum, he refused, and around half the company left. This part relies mostly on Tara’s account, and Sam gets to give his side.

So in this first episode, members of the EA community are both the people who said “making a lot of money to give it away is good” and the people who tried to bring back reason and a careful use of funds.

The series also shows that, as Sam became famous, the community put him on a pedestal, even though, according to Tara, Alameda had made no donations during her time there. She says Sam warned her that the community would believe his version over hers. She describes feeling vulnerable after leaving, with her place in the EA community and her whole social life at stake, and starting to doubt herself as the community held him up as a model.

As the series tells it, the initial motivations are clear: these are very altruistic people, Sam included. Around him are people who want to have a positive impact: Tara; Wayne Hsiung, an animal rights activist active on the EA Forum, who pushed back against earning to give; and later Nishad Singh, an early Alameda employee who went on to head engineering at FTX, who complains that they still haven’t started giving.

After the split, the company turns more and more towards people willing to take risks. Most of the new hires were not looking to have an impact; they just wanted to get rich. While the first people involved were, perhaps, altruists, FTX became a money-maximising operation.

Sam keeps reasoning in terms of expected value, for instance arguing that a 20% chance of FTX not being a flop is enough to justify it. Yet none of the people depicted as effective altruists in the series makes this kind of argument, and by then most of the early ones have left. In a way, they come across as the voice of reason. Through Tara’s voice, effective altruism is associated with prudence and with the importance of keeping promises and not deceiving people.

Over the two episodes, Sam goes further and further in pursuit of more money, more profit, without starting to give significantly, and seems more and more detached from any altruistic goal. My personal impression is of a gambler going double or nothing every three months; what the series shows is Sam’s growing delusions of grandeur. The series also points out how little was donated compared with the company’s valuation, criticises the investment in a coal-powered mine on climate grounds, and shows the money spent on advertising. In the show’s narrative, all of this seems tied to the delusions of grandeur Sam develops as the episodes go on.

The relationship with Caroline

His relationship with Caroline Ellison is at the heart of the second episode. The episode ends with the first signs of trouble in Alameda’s management: the firm relies mostly on its own assets, which are far too unstable.

Summary of episodes 1 and 2

This summary of the two episodes was mostly written with AI.

The episode opens at the FTX Crypto Bahamas conference, with celebrities and former world leaders on stage, then cuts to the collapse: Sam Bankman-Fried was found guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy, about $8 billion of customer money is gone, and victims describe their losses. Sam takes part in the series through video calls from federal prison, limited to about 15 minutes a day. He says he wants “to get the truth out there”, even though the truth “has not been kind” to him.

At a summer maths camp he meets Sam Trabucco and Gary Wang, who both play a role later. Trabucco remembers a teenager already talking about utilitarianism and expected value.
